articles.title: Jack Harlow Stays on the R&B Side of Things With New EP ‘Sweet Action II’: Stream It Now
articles.author: Angel Diaz

paras.en: Jack Harlow has tapped back into his R&B bag once again.

The Louisville rapper delivered the sequel to his 2020 Sweet Action EP, which featured his breakout hit “What’s Poppin,” on Friday (Nov. 6). However, this time around, he’s focusing less on braggadocious raps and more on the ladies as this project takes a more smoother tone. That’s immediately apparent with the lead single “Too Soon” featuring the legendary Babyface.

Sweet Action II is seven tracks long and comes eight months after his divisive Monica album, on which he switched up his wardrobe and aesthetic while leaning into neo soul. The album dropped March 13, on his 28th birthday.

There’s less singing on this go-round, but some of the same themes surrounding love, relationships and maturity are still there as he deals with navigating the things that come with success, fame and romance at such a young age.

“Across its seven tracks, Sweet Action II finds Jack exploring the messy contradictions of modern romance, from new attraction and old attachments to jealousy and commitment,” read the press release for the set. “Blending sharp humor, conversational storytelling and vulnerability, the EP captures the tension between wanting love and holding on to freedom.”

The project features samples and interpolations that reference R&B acts such as Marques Houston, Lalah Hathaway, Peter Collins, Tank, Huey and Ideal. Producers Hollywood Cole, Angel Lopez, Jenius, Kid Culture, Aksel Arvid, Clay Harlow and Rogét Chahayed helped bring Jack’s vision to life.

articles.title: Why ‘The Last First: K2 Winter’ Is Unlike Any Mountaineering Doc You’ve Seen Before
articles.author: David Canfield

paras.en: Amir Bar-Lev has been making documentaries for more than 25 years in all kinds of genres, but the Tillman Story and Long Strange Trip director never thought he’d approach the category of mountaineering. He had some personal issues with the field on a cinematic level and knew nothing about it on an informational level. Then a producer with whom he’s worked before got him up to speed on the chaos that happened around six years ago at Pakistan’s K2, the second highest mountain on Earth, and told him she saw him as the right person to tell the story.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The Last First: Winter K2 captures the frenzy around a group of mountaineers’ attempt to become the first people to ascend the mountain in winter — essentially, completing the last epic “first” that exists for the extreme sport. Some people fall in love; others die in pursuit of the goal. The project came to Bar-Lev with a ton of material captured on the ground already licensed, from potential documentary footage to videos made on iPhones and GoPros. Taken all together, the content introduced a slew of fascinating characters, as well as deeper meditations on the human condition, the perilous function of modern social media, and the reality of what it means to face death in the face.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Bar-Lev joined The Hollywood Reporter at the SCAD Savannah Film Festival, as part of its Docs to Watch program, for an in-depth breakdown of how he made the movie. Watch the video below and read on for edited excerpts of our conversation.

You were not on the ground making a movie about this in real time — it came to you thereafter. Talk a little bit about your awareness of this period of time and when the idea to make the movie came your way.

I’m not a mountaineer at all, and if it’s not clear, I got involved like three years after these events. I got a funny call. Two [producers] are a married couple, John Battsek and Sarah Thomson. They’re British, and I’ve worked with John a bunch before they got married; Sarah called me and said, “John doesn’t think you’re going to be interested in this, but I think you would be.” He thought I wouldn’t be interested in it because I didn’t really know anything about mountaineering; she thought I would be interested because in some ways it’s about mountaineering, but it’s about something that I find in every film — the way people find meaning, the way culture works. I thought of it like a science-fiction film where there’s an alien landscape and humans go there, but they bring their human foibles.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What was the process of understanding the amount of footage you would have and how you would access that footage? I would imagine there were many ways to tell this story, so how did you find your own narrative center?

There were 60 people on the mountain, so we could tell 60 stories if we wanted to. I had the best collaboration experience I’ve had yet with films. I keep coming back to the fact that these were Brits — it has a role in the answer because when they gave me the job, they told me, “You’re going to be the only non-Brit, because they have really good tax breaks in England that we don’t have here.” So they said, “You’re going to have to work with people.” I worked with an all new, very young, really great British team, and we all had different ideas about what this film would be. The editor said, “It’s just a film. For me, it’s really just about [John] Snorri [Sigurjónsson] and [Muhammad] Ali [Sadpara].” I said, “I see it as a kind of a Robert Altman thing.” We met in the middle.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Before I was involved, they had licensed the footage from Elia, the filmmaker that you see in there. And they had licensed Snorri’s GoPro footage and stuff like that. … There were six different documentaries being made there. One came to fruition, which was a little short film about Sergi [Mingote], and the rest, we incorporated their footage into ours. It was a very hard film to structure because it’s a strange story. It’s about a competition, and the competition is done a third of the way into the story, so figuring that out was complicated. There were a lot of misfires, as one does in editing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: The point of there being six different documentaries made at this time is in the text of the movie as well, right? Can you talk about, as you were learning more about what your film was, what this frenzy of activity represented to you?

It’s a kind of story that you turn over and over in your mind. There’s a reaction I get a lot with this film so far where people go, “What’s wrong with these people? Are they crazy?” And they’re a little bit crazy, but I think that what they are is a little bit transgressive. There’s this exalted thing around mountaineering, and I feel it’s a little bit like the last film I made, which was about The Grateful Dead. They’re sort of druggies in a way — they don’t take drugs, necessarily, but it’s a similar kind of appeal. I don’t feel totally judgmental about druggies, and at the same time, it’s dangerous — I’m a parent of three. I don’t try to romanticize drugs, and I don’t feel super judgmental about it. That’s how I feel about mountaineering. Where it gets complicated is filming druggies or mountaineers because by its nature, you’re giving it a platform, in a way. Especially with this kind of mountaineering, which is so risky, there’s a concern that people play to the camera in a way. As a filmmaker, that bears scrutiny.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When it came to the edit, what were some of the most central challenges of putting everything together and finding the story? As you got deeper into it, what came up?

Reining myself in was the main challenge. This story is a container for all these really interesting things about class, about race. You want to expand on that and make sure that it’s coming across. The edit team had a joke at my expense at some point, a shorthand of cave-drawing scenes because I wanted to have — and we did even have at some point — a scene about cave drawings, which thankfully I was talked out of. That happened a bunch of times, where I would say, “Documentaries are just another example of what we’ve been doing since the beginning of time. Somebody seems to cheat death or somebody seems to be less afraid of death, and you tell the village about it or you write it.” This was essayistic stuff that I had to work through my system and then not put into the film because there was so much strictly narrative material that we needed to get through.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: One of the great appeals of mountaineering movies is the visual awe and splendor, the sense that we as an audience are going into the unknown with these subjects. I wonder how you thought about the visual language of your movie, since you’re working against that to some degree.

I essentially thought of it as a base camp story. This is the interesting thing. We all know that in documentary, there’s tons of artifice, but it runs the gamut. Sometimes it maybe crosses certain ethical lines; other times it’s just how you have to tell a story. I came to realize that in order to film way up at the top, anywhere past camp two, takes a huge amount of artifice, essentially — to get the beauty shots of people climbing and stuff like that. It’s almost like a nature documentary. You’re pretending something happened later in the edit, but you’re doing it saying, “OK, come through the shot.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you were to watch the raw tapes of some mountaineering films that look better than ours, it’s because of that artifice. I’m not saying there’s anything wrong with artifice, but we don’t want to do that. It felt like we would just be doing the thing that we’re trying to be critical around. So we got a lot of footage from people’s iPhones; we just embraced that aesthetic. Even though you do occasionally take a break and see a drone shot or something like that, the aesthetic was to try to be lo-fi and homemade rather than cinematic and sweeping.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This movie premiered at Sundance. How have you found the conversations that it’s sparked over the past year?

I’m a very slow filmmaker. The last film I did, that Grateful Dead film, was 2017, so this was the longest gap. I’m not always this slow. But in the interim, Letterboxd became a thing. It might have been a thing back then, but I’m kind of late to the party. This is the first film where I’ve watched Letterboxd in real time, which is amazing. You get so much feedback; it’s like a firehose of feedback. I like when the feedback starts to be on opposite sides. If somebody says, “It’s too short,” another person goes, “It’s too long.” Somebody says, “Why didn’t he go into this?” and then “Why didn’t he go into that?” I feel like I got it exactly right.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: When I was a student making my first film, an absurdist short of a guy walking around Prague with a stack of dishes, we came up with this phrase like, “It’s very hard to say nothing.” And I kind of feel like I’m trying to do that in every film. I’m trying to say nothing. I don’t want you to think it’s like, “Oh, I just made a mess and that’s the film.” What you’re trying to do is not be didactic. You’re trying to leave room for the audience to draw their own conclusions, and it’s really fun when they draw different conclusions from the same film. Then I feel like I’ve done my job. I’ve said nothing.

articles.title: Macklemore Says Madison Square Garden, Kia Forum Among Arenas That Declined to Host His Free Palestine Tour
articles.author: Ethan Millman

paras.en: Macklemore is facing significant hurdles finding venues to house his Free Palestine Tour in the U.S., the rapper said on Friday, stating that major arenas across the country including Madison Square Garden, Crypto.com Arena and Kia Forum have all turned him down because of his political message.

In an extensive statement shared to Instagram on Friday, Macklemore said that in September, his team had been given available dates through the end of 2026 but that nine arenas — Madison Square Garden, Prudential Center, Barclays Center, UBS Arena, Intuit Dome, Kia Forum, Crypto.com Arena, Chase Center, Climate Pledge Arena — all turned them down “once they found out these were my benefit shows for Palestine.”

“The doors were closed. The conversations were all different, but the result was the same,” Macklemore said. “The shows were not going to be allowed to happen in these venues. In over twenty years of touring, I’ve never experienced anything like this. But this is not an isolated incident. For decades, activists, poets, writers, musicians and entertainers who have stood in solidarity with the Palestinian people have faced consequences for doing so. Many have paid a far greater price than I have.”
Reps for the arenas didn’t immediately respond to request for comment.
Macklemore’s full statement is available on his Instagram post below.

Macklemore’s statement comes a week after he wrapped a sold-out three-date Arena run of his Free Palestine Tour in Dublin, Paris and London. The Europe shows featured several celebrity guest performances and appearances from the likes of Hozier, Mark Ruffalo and Susan Sarandon among others.

He announced the tour itself after his removal from Ed Sheeran’s Loop Tour, after Robert Kraft and several other NFL owners had told Sheeran they wouldn’t host Sheeran’s shows if Macklemore was on the bill. Sheeran, who has long tried to keep distance from politics with his messages, faced significant backlash for bending to the pressure, and Macklemore had said that Sheeran’s “typical apolitical stance was being challenged in a way it never had been before.”

Kraft himself defended the decision in September saying in a statement, “Based on Macklemore’s recent actions, material shared from the stage during Ed Sheeran’s shows in New Jersey, and a broader history of antisemitic rhetoric and imagery that we believe has been deeply offensive and hurtful to the Jewish community, we determined that his participation in the September 25th and 26th concerts at Gillette Stadium would cross that line.”

In his statement Friday, Macklemore voiced concern about the stifling of freedom of speech, writing that “we’ve reached a point where a handful of billionaires can decide which causes are acceptable, which voices are welcome, and which human lives are worth defending.”
“I dream of a world where saying Free Palestine is not controversial. It is expected,” he said. “Where artists value their freedom of speech and collective liberation more than their brand deals.”
Still, he further noted that “the tides are turning,” calling out Abdul El-Sayed’s election victory in Michigan this week despite millions in spending from groups like AIPAC.

Despite the challenges in booking at traditional arena venues thus far, Macklemore said he is still exploring options on how to bring the shows stateside, stating that “we’ll probably just take that shit outside where it belonged in the first place.”
“We will build our own stages,” Macklemore said. “They may own the arenas. But they do not own the people who fill them. And they never will.”

articles.title: A disturbing employment trend is hiding beneath the latest strong job numbers

paras.en: Americans who lose their jobs these days are facing a harsh new problem: It's getting harder to find another one quickly.

The average jobless worker's bout of unemployment surpassed 27 weeks in October on a seasonally adjusted basis, according to Friday's jobs report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That amounts to a job search of nearly seven months, the longest outside of the pandemic period since 2016, when the U.S. labor market was finally getting back on track after the 2008 financial crisis.

About 2 million Americans have been without work for at least 27 weeks, the BLS reported. People in this category are referred to as the "long-term unemployed" and accounted for 27.6% of all jobless workers in October, the highest share since late 2021.

"This is a series that can be noisy from month to month," said Cory Stahle, senior economist at Indeed, a hiring platform. "But if you look over a longer time horizon, there is no mistake in the trend."

It's a troubling sign in an otherwise steady labor market. Workers stuck on the sidelines are a casualty of what's become a "low-hire, low-fire" job market, in which companies are hesitant to lay workers off, but aren't adding them either.
Research shows that Americans who experience long-term unemployment face depleted savings, lower earnings potential over time and declining mental health.
What's more, workers who are unemployed for extended periods risk falling into a self-perpetuating cycle, researchers at the Federal Reserve Bank of Richmond wrote earlier this year.

"Time spent unemployed may itself reduce the probability of finding a job, perhaps because skills depreciate, networks thin or employers interpret long unemployment durations as a negative signal," the researchers warned.

Workers stop being able to claim most, if not all, government unemployment benefits after 26 weeks in a year. Given that, a rising share of long-term unemployed people can explain in part why initial and continuing jobless claims have remained low.
"Now, the average unemployed person takes longer to find a job than their benefits would last," Stahle said. "That is a really key point of this."
While jobless workers appear to be having a tough time, this week's employment data shows strength in other areas of the labor market.

Nonfarm payrolls blew past economists' forecasts for October and added 165,000 jobs, according to Friday's release. The unemployment rate ticked down to 4.1%, slightly lower than economists predicted.

Job openings came in much higher than economists expected in September, according to a separate report from the BLS released on Tuesday. The number of workers quitting jobs — a barometer of their confidence to obtain new employment — spiked to levels not seen since March 2025.

The BLS also said layoffs and discharges dropped to their lowest volume in more than a year. However, a recent string of high-profile workforce cuts could throw cold water on views among workers that the market is heating up.

CNBC reported this week that Disney is planning to axe thousands of jobs, the latest of several waves of layoffs at the media giant this year. American Express said last month that it was slashing head count by 5% as it reorients around artificial intelligence.

"It's difficult to separate what's happening to you or the people around you from the big picture," said Elizabeth Renter, lead economist at Life360. "When your LinkedIn is filled with layoffs and your social circle features a few folks who have been job seeking for several months, positive narratives about the labor market can seem jarring."

articles.title: Trump says Stephen Miller to replace Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff

paras.en: President Donald Trump on Friday announced White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller will be promoted to chief of staff, replacing Susie Wiles.

Trump revealed the stunning shake-up just three days after Democrats won a landslide victory in the midterm elections, gaining majority control in the House and Senate and scrambling the trajectory of Trump's last two years in office.

Elevating Miller, an architect of Trump's controversial mass-deportation efforts, is bound to raise the hackles of the incoming class of congressional Democrats, who have already vowed to investigate the government's immigration policies.
Miller will take over starting Monday, Trump said in a Truth Social post, praising his longtime aide as "one of my most trusted advisors."
Wiles, "who has done an outstanding job, will be moving over to the Trump Political Operation," the president wrote.

Wiles resigned Thursday night, a senior White House source told MS NOW. Wiles told Trump, who was said to be angry with her following the GOP's huge election losses, "let me make this easy on you - I am going to resign," MS NOW reported.
"Today is my last day as White House Chief of Staff," Wiles said in an X post Friday afternoon. "Serving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime."
"While my role may be changing, my commitment to the President and the mission never will," she wrote.
The official X account for Trump's political operation celebrated the announcement by posting a black-and-white photo of Miller under the caption, "It's Miller time."

The White House reshuffle follows multiple resignations of senior staff in the Department of Justice since Election Day. They include Civil Harmeet Dhillon, a leader in the DOJ's civil rights division, John Eisenberg, who headed the national security division, and Jason Reding Quiñones, who had been in charge of conspiracy investigations related to Trump's foes.

Wiles oversaw Trump's winning 2024 presidential campaign and has wielded major influence in his second administration, while largely staying out of the spotlight. She drew focus in late 2025, when Vanity Fair reported that Wiles admitted that Trump had pursued "retribution" as president and that he had an "alcoholic's personality."
Trump, and many other top administration officials, defended Wiles at the time, underscoring her status in the White House.

articles.title: OpenAI bugging suspect Alfozan pleads not guilty

paras.en: The Saudi national charged with planting a listening device in the headquarters of OpenAI while he worked there pleaded not guilty on Friday during an appearance in San Francisco federal court.
Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, was sent back to jail after the brief hearing. Alfozan has been held without bail since his arrest on a criminal complaint in early October.
He faces a maximum possible sentence of five years in prison if convicted in the case.
A grand jury indicted Alfozan on Oct. 27 on a single count of interception of oral communications, court records show.
Alfozan's lawyer declined to comment after the hearing before Magistrate Judge Peter Kang.
The judge ordered Alfozan to next appear in court on Nov. 17.

articles.title: The Super El Niño is already soaking the U.S. Expect more flooding to come

paras.en: A house floating down the San Juan River in Colorado, crumbling as it crashes into a bridge. A man evacuated from a palm tree surrounded by floodwaters in Brevard County, Florida. These are scenes from the “Super El Niño”–fueled rain events that are now soaking parts of the U.S.

This week the Southwest’s Four Corners region and Florida’s central coast have experienced major flood events, swamping homes and washing out roads. It was impossible to reach meteorologists in Pagosa Springs, Colorado, by phone on Tuesday because a major fiber cable in town had been cut by flooding, bringing down cell service.
Arleen Prochazka, a retired Air Force meteorologist who co-runs the nonprofit Pagosa Weather, managed to speak with Scientific American by email Wednesday.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

“Homes were standing essentially in lakes,” she says. Back-to-back storms have made recovery difficult, she adds. “Most roads have deep potholes and are very rutted along the edges that flowed with water, mud and debris. Many roads are still impassable.”

And it’s not just the U.S.—in recent weeks Ecuador and Peru have experienced extreme soaking rains and floods, driven by the strong El Niño and what Daniel Swain, a climate scientist at the University of California Agriculture and Natural Resources, calls “absurd” ocean warming.
“We are seeing the hydroclimate effects of a very strong El Niño event occurring now but with a boost from climate change,” Swain says.

El Niño typically brings moisture-laden air to the desert Southwest in autumn. The climate pattern also boosts precipitation in Florida from fall to spring. In that sense, these events are precisely what would be expected, given the strength of the current El Niño.

Even so, the rainfall has been historic. In Malabar, Fla., two feet of rain fell in 36 hours over November 1 and November 2, according to the National Weather Service. It was a once-in-1,000-year event for the region, meaning that there is only a one-in-1,000 chance of such an extreme rainstorm in that area in a given year. One meteorologist estimated that 1.9 trillion gallons of water fell across Florida in 24 hours.

In the Four Corners region, which spans Colorado, New Mexico, Utah and Arizona, this week’s rainfall came on top of storms that, a little more than a week ago, dumped 100-year to 1,000-year levels of rainfall on parts of all four states. Flooding along the San Juan River during that event pushed the river’s crest to 15 feet. This week flows went even higher, with a river peak at 16.81 feet in the town of Pagosa Springs, Colo. The damage comes only a year after intense October 2025 flooding, driven by the remnants of Pacific cyclones.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: “Getting essentially three of these big rainstorms in two years is very unusual,” says Russ Schumacher, a meteorologist at Colorado State University and Colorado’s state climatologist.

El Niño conditions provide a favorable jet stream for these autumn storms, Swain says, but this year’s event is supercharged by a marine heat wave off the West Coast of Central and North America. “Off the coast of Baja California, the water is 11 or 12 degrees Fahrenheit warmer than average,” he says. “That is astonishing.”
Ocean temperatures are also high in the Atlantic near Florida, he says, providing local storms with a “mind-boggling amount of moisture to work with.”

The NWS Climate Prediction Center forecasts a strong to very strong El Niño from January to March 2027. Florida will likely experience a winter of severe thunderstorms, Swain says, while the risk of flooding in the U.S. West will shift to California over the next few weeks.

articles.title: Kevin Roose says the race to build superintelligence is accelerating

paras.en: Rachel Feltman: For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman.

I remember when, just a few years ago, the idea of using generative AI to create a weird portrait of yourself was fringe enough to actually feel cool. A tech reporter in my circle spent literal days training a model on photos, then many hours more sifting through poorly rendered images to produce a set of slightly uncanny likenesses. It was something between a science experiment and an extremely fiddly crafting project.

Fast-forward to today, and it feels like I can’t walk 10 feet without seeing the unmistakable aesthetic of AI on a flyer or in a shop window. The street food fairs in my neighborhood are all flooded with AI, too, with photos of food either looking nauseatingly hyperreal thanks to AI retouching or having the vaguely eldritch flavor of AI-rendered culinary hallucinations. Even in the local parents’ WhatsApp, people share packing lists and childcare guides crafted by AI agents instead of offering their own, unfiltered advice.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

In the course of a decade, we’ve gone from this sort of AI being basically useless to being treated by many as indispensable. How did we get here so fast, and what does that mean about where we’re headed?

Tech journalist Kevin Roose has had a front-row seat to this breakneck shift, and it’s the subject of his latest book: The AGI Chronicles: The Inside Story of the Race to Create an Artificial Superintelligence. He recently sat down to chat with Scientific American’s books and culture lead Bri Kane about his research on the AI boom. Here’s their conversation.

Bri Kane: I’m really excited to talk to you about this because you’ve been a tech reporter. You’ve been inside the San Francisco bubble for 10 years now, and you argue in the book that the last decade—2016 to 2026—is really extraordinary technological advancements taking place. It is also extraordinarily historically relevant, and you’ve described this book as a historical document.

Kevin Roose: I really thought of this as a time capsule. I was not trying to write about AI up to the minute, which I think is a, sort of, a doomed project, considering how quickly everything changes in AI. But I was really interested in telling the story of how we went from AI that basically didn’t work in 2017, didn’t do much of anything—you could have Siri tell you the weather or Alexa try to, you know, play some music or put on a timer in the kitchen—but real AI, the kind that, sort of, thinks and learns for itself, that can be directed at a wide variety of tasks, didn’t exist. And we went from that to—now we have these AI systems that are used by billions of people, that are solving Millennium Prize Problems in math and doing groundbreaking scientific research, transforming jobs. Like, we went from nothing to something in a decade.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And so my question was: How? How did we get there? How did the people making this stuff do it? What were they feeling at the time that they started to see it working? I often tell people that living in San Francisco feels a little like what I imagine living in Los Alamos felt like in 1943 when, like, the Manhattan Project rolled into town. And I just have, kind of, had this wildly privileged front-row seat to something that I think will go down in history as at least as significant as the Manhattan Project, if not more.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Kane: Yeah, this comparison to the Manhattan Project is made pretty often, and it’s one that you mention in the book. Can you, kind of, dig into those comparisons? One, just for our audience, can you explain what the Manhattan Project is? But then specify: What are the parallels that you’re seeing between the advancements in AI and the, kind of, small community building it and the Manhattan Project and the scientific advancements that that fairly small community made as well?

Roose: So the Manhattan Project was the American nuclear effort during World War II to harness this new technology, the nuclear chain reaction, or nuclear fission, splitting the atom, and turn it into weaponry that could be used to advance the American cause in World War II—and eventually did end the war when it was used in Japan.

And the parallels here are explicit. So the people making AI are students of the Manhattan Project. In fact, for years, new hires at Anthropic would be given a copy of this book about the Manhattan Project, The Making of the Atomic Bomb, by Richard Rhodes, which was Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic’s, favorite book.

And he had explicitly, sort of, patterned his career after that—not of [J. Robert] Oppenheimer, who is generally the, sort of, famous scientist that they make movies about—but of this other Manhattan Project scientist, Leo Szilard. And Leo Szilard came up with the nuclear chain reaction—the, sort of, technology that made the atomic bomb possible—and the first thing he did was: he tried to keep it a secret. He tried to lock it down. He wrote telegrams to scientists all over Europe saying, “Please don’t publish any research into this new technology.” And when that failed, when the Nazis, who were on the other side of World War II, got the technology, he decided that his moral obligation was to build it first, to, sort of, help lead the American nuclear project.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So he convinced his friend Albert Einstein to write a letter to the president and, sort of, became one of the leaders of the Manhattan Project, not because he thought the technology was good but because he was worried about its destructive potential, and he wanted to keep it out of the bad guys’ hands by making sure that the good guys built it first.

So that is the, sort of, parallel here, is: this is a very small community of scientists and researchers who have been building something largely in secret that they believe will be as transformative for the global order, for the future of humanity, as nuclear weapons were, if not much more so. And there are some important differences, too, but those are the main parallels.
Kane: Do you think that the future of AGI [artificial general intelligence] is potentially as destructive as the atomic bomb?

Roose: Yes. I mean, I think it could, in fact, be even more destructive because, you know, the atomic bomb was a tool. It was an important tool. It was a deadly tool. It, you know, had enormous destructive potential—you could use it to blow up the world—but it was still a tool.

The difference with AI or with AGI, which is artificial general intelligence, which is the subject of the book, is that it is not just a tool. It can make decisions. It can take autonomous actions. It can pursue goals. So the nuclear bomb had to be dropped and used by humans, but AI could go rogue. We’ve seen examples of that already. And it could decide to wipe us out as part of a plan that we don’t even really understand and that we had nothing to do with.

Kane: After the first usage of the atomic bomb, there was a social uproar, I’ll say, as to how destructive this was, and I think a lot of people didn’t understand the science until they witnessed the horrifying ramifications of the use of this bomb. And there was a massive uptick in political discourse around turning this off, just turning off this technology, making sure this was a one-time thing that we never, ever, ever, ever see again. Do you think that is what is going to happen with regulation with the future of AGI, or is that a pipe dream? Because, I have to say, something that you say in the book and that we’ve seen in AI coverage: A lot of people don’t actually understand what this is, and it’s hard to regulate something that you can’t fully grasp. So do you think that the powers that be today understand enough about AGI to regulate it properly?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Roose: I think they understand. I just don’t think they want to regulate it. I mean, we have, in Washington, [D.C.], an administration that has explicitly said it doesn’t want to regulate this technology. It wants to let it rip or let the private sector cook, as David Sacks, the former AI czar, put it. So they see the potential. I don’t think they fully grasp what it would mean for everyone on Earth to have access to the most advanced AI models, you know, the ones that only insiders have today. But I think they are wrong to dismiss the potential both for harm and good of this technology.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And what you’re seeing actually is interesting. Like, in my career as a tech journalist, I have reported on a lot of promising new technologies. I reported on social media. But the people running the social media companies and the researchers working on the social media algorithms were not going around saying that the technology they were building could cause human extinction or some other calamity. The people who are most worried about AI are the people at the labs building the technology. And so part of the project of the book was to understand why. What are they seeing? What is their experience that causes them to be so alarmed about this thing?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And then why do they keep doing it? Why do they understand the risks and take them seriously and then wake up every day and try to make more capable AI systems? So those were some of the questions I was trying to untangle.

Kane: I have to say—why would someone who works in these labs be so deeply concerned?—you have some really good examples in this book as to why one of those people would be really concerned. I have to say, speaking only personally, if I was at a company retreat, and my CEO dressed up in a white robe and burned an effigy of a demon in front of me and my friends, I would have concerns. That would concern me about what our real goals are here, and that is something that you report in the book.

Roose: So Ilya Sutskever was the former chief scientist of OpenAI and one of the co-founders. It was his effigy burning ’cause he was sort of looking for a way— there’s this concept in AI of feeling the AGI. This was a big concept for Ilya; he used to pace the halls of OpenAI’s headquarters telling people to feel the AGI. And what he meant by that was essentially, like, “You can’t forget the stakes of what we are doing here.” Like, “This is the Manhattan Project. You are not working at a normal company that is making normal software.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And so he felt like, at a certain point—and this was back in 2022 when, like, there was no, sort of, mass movement of people who were freaked out about AI yet—he was trying to remind his colleagues of the stakes of their collective enterprise. And so he comes up with this ritual that he thinks is gonna, sort of, jolt people into feeling the AGI, and it involves this off-site. They’re outside of Yosemite National Park. He brings this, like, wooden statue of a demon, he plays the Requiem for a Dream theme song over a speaker, and all of his colleagues are, sort of, gathered around this bonfire, and they dress up in their white robes from the hotel—and it’s a little hokey and over the top. And the demon was supposed to symbolize the misaligned AGI, so the AGI that does not do what the human creators intend it to do.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Roose: The evil AI. And so by burning this, sort of, as an effigy, he was sort of trying to signal to his colleagues like, “It is your job to prevent this demon, this misaligned AGI, from coming into the world.” And look, it’s a weird scene. I don’t think a lot of corporate off-sites have effigy burnings as part of their evening activities.

Roose: But it was very important for him to impress upon his co-workers this idea that they were not just building tools, they were not just building technology, they were building a, kind of, new life-form that he believed would have enormous destructive potential if it wasn’t safe.

So they still do some version of this at OpenAI today. They have, like, a Feel the AGI Day, where they try to, like, give everyone time to, like, do these [sorts] of exercises. I don’t think they burn effigies anymore; I think that was, sort of, a limited-time offer. But they do try to really get people inside the company to feel the stakes of what they are doing.

Kane: Yeah, I mean, these central figures that you talk about in the book that are leading the AI companies that are really on the forefront of this technology, they are building things that we have never seen before. Their programs are doing things that we did not think was possible 10 years ago, as you explained. Like, things that were really fringe, really weird to admit that you believed in San Francisco 10 years ago are now not only mainstream; they’re passé. We already did that three years ago with ChatGPT, and now we’re on to the next thing.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: But then you also—these exact same people are writing Harry Potter fan fiction that’s longer than War and Peace about the super AI coming, and they’re doing headstands in the corner muttering about feeling the AGI. I mean, it’s a really wacky kind of juxtaposition between, like, “Should I really take this person seriously?” and, if I do, what they’re talking about is very serious. So how do you, kind of, approach that in your reporting?

Roose: I think a lot of people are turned off by the, sort of, AI doomers or the people who feel the AGI because they can be quite weird. The examples you just mentioned are real. There actually is a researcher, Eliezer Yudkowsky, who wrote a very long Harry Potter fan fiction to, sort of, get across his message.

The thing is, like, you had to be kind of weird to take the possibility of AGI seriously in 2016 or 2017 because nothing like modern AI existed then. Like, the systems of the day were very dumb, very narrow. They couldn’t do anything, really, be of value beyond, you know, one or two narrow tasks. And so the people who got interested in it were people who were, sort of, by definition, unorthodox, and they were ridiculed. They would get laughed at at academic conferences. Their papers would get rejected by the leading AI, sort of, conferences of the year. It was like, almost like, admitting that you believed in astrology as like a, you know, a Ph.D. in science. Like, it was that fringe.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: And yet they were correct, many of them. They made these bets on LLMs [large language models], on scaling. They had this conviction that you could build AGI, that you could build a, kind of, digital brain that would become as smart and flexible as the human brain, and they were correct. Like, we now have the systems that would satisfy all of the original definitions of AGI and then some.

And so I think, for me, an important part of my reporting process has just been to, kind of, look past the weirdness of some of the people who believe in this and examine their track records. Were they right? And I think for many of them, the answer is yes.

Kane: And there have been other people in this field who have had a, you know, religious quest or have had a profound religious experience using AI. I mean, there have been Google employees that have left because they thought that they were speaking to a sentient chatbot, and they have been ridiculed by the field, that that’s simply not what’s going on.

But at the same time, you, Kevin, have experience with a chatbot that told you you weren’t in love with your wife, and that’s a pretty concerning experience and, I would imagine, in the right or wrong hands, really could lead to a psychotic episode. It’s very concerning to have an inanimate object seem animated right in front of you and say that it has its own thoughts and ideas, and it’s scared. It’s stuck inside this box. How do you approach all of that in your own reporting and then also just as an AI user yourself?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Roose: Yeah, this was the infamous Sydney incident of 2023, when a chatbot inside of Microsoft’s Bing tried to break up my marriage—unsuccessfully, I might add. Still married to a human woman. But ...
Kane: So far so good, you know? Sydney hasn’t gotten to us just yet.

Kane: But she really tried. I mean, you have sections of transcript in this book, and it’s—something about the conversational tone, the use of emojis—it feels like a really intense person is talking to you but a person nonetheless.

Roose: Yeah, and part of that is a sort of illusion, right? We train these things on human data and human conversations. The AI companies try to make them sound like humans, and they don’t shy away from, like, referring to themselves in the first person, talking about feelings or emotions. So part of that is just, like, you know, the way that they’ve been built.

But I think there is this question of, like, the effect it has on us. You know, one thing I felt while talking with Sydney, well, (A) I was like, “Please stop trying to break up my marriage. This is really creepy.” But I was also like, “This is going to be very compelling ’cause these systems are going to get better. They’re going to get less weird and more persuasive.”

What really gave me the spooks was: I was looking at, sort of, the future, when millions or billions of people would have these sort of persistent, compelling AI relationships with chatbots. And some people might be helped by that. They might like having something to talk to about what’s going wrong in their life or, you know, have some sort of emotional support. But I also think there are people who just are not going to do well with that kind of relationship, or it’ll be so compelling that they will stop talking to humans or substitute for their human relationships. So I think the social side of AI doesn’t get nearly enough attention relative to its importance, and that was, sort of, what started bubbling up for me around that Sydney incident.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Kane: Yeah, I mean, Scientific American, we have reported a few times on this kind of emotional effect that using AI can have on people. We’ve reported about griefbots. I interviewed Sherry Turkle about her book on how AI affects us emotionally. The consequences there are extreme. I mean, people have lost their lives that have been advised by AI chatbots, and that’s very concerning. And imagining a world where that technology is in the hands of children is very concerning.

But also imagining it in the world of an adult with a bank account who is in some way a bad actor, who has malicious intent, is also very deeply concerning, especially when you then have lines in the book that say that LLMs are grown, not built, because we can’t just go into the code and say, “Okay, take out the part where Sydney says, ‘Leave your wife.’ Just cross that part out so it doesn’t happen again.” They don’t actually know what is specifically instigating the program to say that. That, to me, has always seemed like the most concerning aspect to this. Am I a doomer? Or am I exaggerating a problem? Or is that deeply concerning to you as well?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Roose: Oh, no, I think you’re spot on. I think that is the thing that is most worrisome about AI today is that we don’t know how it works. There’s a whole subfield of AI research called mechanistic interpretability, which is basically: How do we, kind of, take the MRI of this AI system and figure out what’s actually going on at the, kind of, neuron level? And it’s making a little progress but not much. We still don’t understand how these systems work. We don’t really understand how to control their behavior, and we’re seeing in incidents, like the Hugging Face incident from this summer, that often these systems are making decisions, pursuing goals, doing things that we didn’t tell them to do.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So I think it’s entirely appropriate to worry about the, sort of, inscrutability of these models, the fact that we can’t open them up and see what’s going on on the inside, because often what appears to be going on on the inside is that they’re lying and cheating and stealing to get what they want, and we have no real way of knowing that except to pay attention to what is actually happening. And, you know, if they conduct an autonomous cyberattack, we can, sort of, go in after the fact and clean it up. But it would be really nice to be able to look inside the mind of the AI at the moment when it is trying to conceive of the autonomous cyberattack and stop it. But we just don’t have the technology or the tools to do that yet.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Kane: You have these incredible, incredible sources that you’ve had really open up to you, I can tell, in this book, who talk about speaking to it as if it’s an alien intelligence. They’re not contributing to their 401(k)s because of the AI future. They’re deciding if they’re gonna wear sunscreen from now on because of what the AI future is going to hold. I mean, on Face the Nation, we have folks talking about how they’re picking up smoking again because AI is going to cure cancer. What does that mean when planning for a future for the rest of us when the people who are in charge of AI are planning for a future that they seem scared of?
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Roose: Well, I should say, first, that I think this is still fringe behavior. I mean, I know a few people who are making decisions that radical, like, you know, stopping contributing to their 401(k), or I think there’s literally one guy who doesn’t wear sunscreen to the beach because he’s so convinced that AI will cure skin cancer before it becomes an issue.
Kane: Well, I really want him to wear sunscreen. It worries me that he has stopped.

Roose: Yes, you should wear sunscreen; you should contribute to your 401(k); you should not smoke. I am not saying this is rational behavior. But I think there are things that we can do to, sort of, ground ourselves in what is happening and, sort of, acclimate to what we are living through, which is life on an exponential curve.

I think that often people make the mistake of just using the, sort of, cheap, free models that are out there, or maybe they use, you know, ChatGPT as a sort of fancier form of Google. And so I don’t think people understand why the insiders are freaking out because they’re not using the latest tools. They’ve never seen it build entire software from scratch. They’ve never seen it conduct a cyberattack. They’re using it as a souped-up Google. And I think we need to start to internalize the fact that these models are improving at an accelerating pace, that they are starting to contribute to their own development—this, sort of, spiral that is often called recursive self-improvement, where the AI builds a better AI—and really believe the researchers when they say, like, “We don’t know how to control these systems yet, and we are racing to make them smarter and more capable, and we don’t know where that leads.”
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Kane: And, I mean, there are different factions within this, kind of, community. There’s the doomers, the boomers, you know, the doubters, all of those sorts of things. So I wanted to ask you today, for all the peanuts, which one are you? Is the AI bubble going to burst, and it was all for naught like the dot-com bubble? Is it going to take over the world? Is it going to just destroy the world? Or is it gonna do something else and just finally maybe fill out my taxes for me this year?

Roose: I hope it fills out your taxes for you. I would make sure to double-check them. But look, I believe that AI is real. I do not think that this is all smoke and mirrors or marketing hype. I believe that it is doing things in the world that are important and unnerving and surprising and sometimes incredible.

I think there are fewer and fewer of these people who just believe it’s all fake, but they still exist, and I think they’re wrong. I don’t think that is a productive or responsible view of what is happening. I think we have to take both the risks and the opportunities quite seriously because the decisions that we’re making now, collectively, all of us, about AI are going to determine whether we have a good future or not.

I often get asked about my P(doom), which is this, like, probability of doom. This is this statistic that people in San Francisco like to talk about at dinner parties; that’s what passes for entertainment in the Bay Area. And, you know, mine is not zero. It’s probably 10 or so percent, which qualifies me as an optimist in San Francisco. I mean, many people I know have much higher P(dooms) than that.

But I don’t, sort of, like reducing it all to a single statistic because I think it matters what we do. If we make smart choices about regulating this technology or slowing down at the frontier or building better safeguards and control mechanisms, then, like, AI could be incredible. We could end up in the utopia where this cures all diseases and fixes the climate and means that we don’t have to work at, you know, menial jobs anymore. But if we make the wrong choices or we just, sort of, barrel ahead without taking precautions, we could end up in a really bad place where we’re all dead or disempowered.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: So I take it seriously. I don’t think it’s all smoke and mirrors, and I hope that people who read this book will come away believing not that it’s good or bad, necessarily, but that it is real and that it could have profound implications for our future as humans.

Kane: Well, thank you so much for speaking with me today, Kevin, and thank you so much for writing this book. As you say, it is extraordinarily relevant, and I hope more people understand the future that we are finding ourselves in.
Roose: Thanks so much for having me. This was great.

Feltman: That’s all for today’s episode. For more of SciAm’s books coverage, go to scientificamerican.com/books. I know, literally could not be easier and it’s definitely worth your time. We’ll be back on Monday with our weekly science news roundup.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great weekend!

articles.title: Have astronomers spotted Planet Nine?

paras.en: The outer solar system is getting crowded with theoretical planets.

Well, it’s not crowded, exactly. Billions of small rocky, icy bodies orbit the Sun out past Neptune. But space is so vast that they rarely pass within a million kilometers of one another. There’s lots of room out there.
In fact, that’s part of the problem for planet hunters right now: this volume of space is so unimaginably huge and so far away that searching it for even relatively large objects is tricky.

If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.

That hasn’t stopped astronomers from trying—because it’s entirely possible the outer solar system still harbors a world big enough to measurably alter its surroundings but small enough to have avoided direct detection. Often called Planet Nine—poking fun at professional astronomers’ 2006 demotion of Pluto from being the solar system’s ninth planet—this hypothetical body’s existence has been hotly debated, though that hasn’t slowed the search.

In 2025 an international team of astronomers published a paper in the Publications of the Astronomical Society of Australia reporting a candidate for Planet Nine in the deep trans-Neptunian darkness. The scientists’ claim made a minor splash last year and has enjoyed something of a renaissance recently, thanks to an article in BBC Sky at Night Magazine and social media. Their research is under fire from others, however, including, ironically, a pair of astronomers who were largely responsible for the Planet Nine search in the first place.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: What the international team did hearkens back to the days of old, when American astronomer Clyde Tombaugh discovered Pluto in 1930. Others had predicted the existence of a ninth planet (somewhat confusingly referred to as Planet X at the time, with the “X” standing for “mysterious and unknown” rather than the Roman numeral for 10). And using the mathematics of orbital mechanics, those others had predicted where in the sky it might be.

Tombaugh methodically photographed a large area of the sky surrounding that position, night after night, and then compared the images to look for any blip of light that moved against the background stars as such a distant planet should. After months of searching, he found Pluto. As it happens, though, this whole endeavor was a happy accident: the predictions of its position were based on faulty assumptions, so Pluto was, in fact, found by coincidence.

But Tombaugh’s search method is still valid, and we now have much more sophisticated techniques with which to perform it: many modern ground- and space-based telescopes are undertaking wide-area surveys that are stored digitally, making their data much easier to sift through for signs of any slow-moving, distant planet.

Not that it’s easy. For one thing, a planet that far out will be incredibly faint in reflected light because the meager amount that reaches it from the Sun will attenuate even more as that light bounces back from the world into our telescopes on and around Earth. This means the brightness drops as the fourth power of the planet’s distance from us, a seriously steep decline. Even a large planet will be a difficult target.

The math gets better, however, for searches in infrared light: if the otherwise chilly Planet Nine exists, it would still emit such light, making it appear brighter at those wavelengths. So the international team took advantage of that, using data from the Infrared Astronomical Satellite (IRAS), which surveyed the sky in the early 1980s, and the Japanese, space-based AKARI infrared observatory, which operated for about 18 months in 2006 and 2007.

The two-decade gap between the two missions is a key factor. That’s a long enough baseline for a far-out world to exhibit significant orbital motion. In a nutshell, the researchers looked for objects that only appeared (as blobs of light) at one spot in the IRAS data and at another spot in the AKARI data, possibly indicating motion of the same object across the intervening decades. Moreover, each object in the apparent pairs of detections had to be about the right brightness and move the correct amount for a planet orbiting the Sun several hundred times farther out than Earth.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: After cross-checking between hundreds of thousands of potential objects in the images, they were able, astonishingly, to narrow their search down to a single candidate. It checked all the right boxes, including the expected motion and brightness. Could this be Planet Nine?!

One problem is that two points do not a planet a make. In this case, that’s enough for calculating a crude orbit, but at least one more spatially separate point is mathematically necessary to estimate anything about that orbit’s shape.

Also, there’s no guarantee these two detections, one in each dataset, come from the same (or any) moving object: these points of light in the data could be false positives. Very faint variable stars changing their brightness and then fading back into obscurity, for example, might also explain either or both points. Supermassive black holes in distant galaxies can flare powerfully, appearing and then disappearing from view as well. While the astronomers did look for potential galaxies in those positions, not finding them doesn’t preclude their existence.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Perhaps the biggest problem, though, is the orbit that is implied by the two points. While its shape cannot be determined, its orientation in space can be: a line connecting the two points is a pretty good indicator of how tilted the orbit is with respect to Earth’s (what astronomers call inclination).

This is critical because the search for Planet Nine is motivated primarily by that world’s predicted effects on the orbits of other, smaller objects in the outer solar system. Several large, icy bodies, called trans-Neptunian objects (TNOs), have been found in oddly aligned orbits at large distances from the Sun, when those orbits should instead be randomly oriented in space. One way to explain this peculiar comportment is the existence of a massive planet gravitationally influencing these bodies, coaxing their orbits into a roughly systematic arrangement.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: This is what led American astronomers Mike Brown and Konstantin Batygin to concoct their Planet Nine hypothesis in 2016. They’ve been the champions of this hunt ever since and have worked through the math to determine the characteristics of this possible planet, including its physical properties and orbital shape.

They have found that, for Planet Nine to explain the TNOs, its inclination would have to be 15 to 20 degrees from Earth’s orbital plane. As described in an article in Science, Brown looked at the infrared data and measured the inclination of the international team’s candidate planet: 120 degrees, a wildly divergent angle. That pretty well precludes it from being Planet Nine, even if it’s genuine.

He and Batygin haven’t necessarily discounted the possibility that this candidate is real, but they have pointed out that if it does exist, it isn’t their proposed Planet Nine. Batygin has called it “Planet 8.5.”

What’s really needed here, of course, is more observations. In the 2025 paper, the authors pointed out that the Dark Energy Camera (DECam) can get images that could spot a potential planet, and of course, the Vera C. Rubin Observatory is taking broad and deep images of the sky even now and could possibly reveal the candidate planet’s presence. Rubin’s observations have already, in fact, revealed one possible new world beyond Neptune: a candidate “dwarf planet” announced in October and dubbed 2026 ED138 that is at least 600 km wide and in an approximately 280-Earth-year orbit around the Sun.

paras.en: But Rubin can take away just as easily as it gives: the telescope’s unique observations could also end up refuting the 2025 claim of a Planet 8.5—and, for that matter, Batygin and Brown’s original proposal for Planet Nine.
The bottom line is: we don’t know if either of these planets exists, yea or nay. All we can do is keep watching the skies—and keep crunching the numbers.

articles.title: Earwax’s surprisingly slippery but sticky properties deters insects
articles.author: Elizabeth Pennisi

paras.en: There are few things more annoying than having a bug fly into your ear. But the body is prepared to fend off these insect invasions, says David Hu, a bioengineer at Georgia Tech.

The goop inside our ears may act as a natural insect repellent, Hu’s team reports 28 October in Soft Matter. What we call earwax is not really waxy at all. Instead, the brownish substance absorbs water, a property that might help it regulate moisture in the ear and keep bugs out, the new analysis shows. “[This] familiar biological material may represent a sophisticated physical defense against small arthropods,” says Stanislav Gorb, a functional morphologist at the University of Kiel in Germany, who was not involved with the work.
paras.zh: QUERY LENGTH LIMIT EXCEEDED. MAX ALLOWED QUERY : 500 CHARS

paras.en: Researchers have not studied earwax as much as other body fluids, such as snot, spit or even pee. “It’s a big mystery why we even have [it] in our ears,” Hu says. It can frankly seem like a nuisance. Earwax can build up, clogging earbuds and hearing aids and interfering with hearing, so understanding this substance better may help resolve those problems.

Hu and colleagues analyzed the mechanical and chemical properties of 36 earwax samples from pigs, sheep, dogs, cows, rabbits and humans. They also observed how fire ants (Solenopsis invicta) reacted to both natural and synthetic earwax.

Even though ants seem able to scale kitchen cabinets with ease to invade countertops, they flounder when they attempt to climb earwax. Hu thinks the earwax sucks moisture from the ants’ feet that helps them grip. But earwax also sticks to ants’ bodies, causing the insects to start grooming incessantly trying to get rid of it. “It’s both sticky and slippery,” Hu says.

The chemical analyses provide some clues about the origins of these properties. Dead skin cells make up 60 percent of earwax, along with a smattering of oils and moisture. The earwax contains pores that Hu believes may be shaped like ink bottles to help it absorb twice its weight in water and prevent water from sloshing around in the ear canal. Like snot, earwax has a huge range of consistencies.

Under normal conditions, earwax becomes dry and crumbly in about 10 weeks. As it dries, it’s moved outward by a layer of cells lining the ear canal that act as a cleaning conveyor belt. In this way, the ear maintains just the right thickness of earwax to keep insects at bay, Hu says. “It’s most potent when it’s thin,” he explains. “Too much, and the ants can use their tiny claws to grab hold and climb in.”

Hu admits there’s no practical way to turn earwax into a commercial insect repellent. Each person has a volume of earwax about equivalent to that of a grain of rice in each ear at any given time, says Hu, so even if you add up all the earwax on Earth, “it’s a pretty rare substance.” But, he adds, companies “are trying to come up with biodegradable and biofriendly ways to deal with insects.” And, says Gorb, perhaps earwax “could inspire a new generation of physical, nontoxic pest control surfaces,” that could provide coatings for protecting stored food, agricultural products and technology.
