paras.en: The first eight launches for Exolaunch in 2026 took place across four different launch vehicles from three continents. By securing capacity across a diverse portfolio of launch vehicles, inclinations, and spaceports, Sproles said, Exolaunch gives launch customers not only more predictable access to orbit, but also increased flexibility with regard to cost, schedule, and orbital destination.

Sproles ultimately envisions a future where customers can launch at any time and to any orbit without ever having to consider available launch vehicles or schedules — just as manufacturers in other industries can ship their products knowing that there’s always a container ship, train, or truck available to transport them.

“The ideal situation is that customers don’t have to think about what the vehicle is or when it’s going because there’s always an option to get to the desired orbit at the time when their satellite is manufactured,” Sproles said.
That future is in the hands of launch companies.

“We have multiple launch providers who have shown they can launch rockets. Now, we need those launchers to launch. We need them operating reliably at cadence, and we need them going to multiple orbits. They can do it. We just need them to execute.”

articles.title: ‘No Escape’ for refugees on the frontlines of the climate crisis

paras.en: ‘No Escape’ for refugees on the frontlines of the climate crisis

The climate emergency is an immediate crisis for refugees, with three in four – nearly 90 million people – living in countries facing high to severe exposure to hazards such as drought, floods and extreme heat.

Vulnerable as they are, climate financing is failing to reach many communities at risk, the UN refugee agency, UNHCR, warned in a report published on Friday ahead of the COP31 climate change conference opening next week in Antalya, Türkiye.

“Refugees face a double injustice. Forced to flee conflicts they did not cause, they are now on the frontlines of a climate crisis they have contributed least to,” said Antón Leis García, Assistant High Commissioner for Operations.
“For millions, climate change is not a distant threat. It is destroying shelters, undermining livelihoods and putting their hopes of rebuilding their lives at risk.”
The report – No Escape III – finds that the fragile and conflict-affected countries that host large refugee populations receive only around 10 per cent of global funding to address climate change.
It highlights the stories of eight representatives from displaced communities on the frontlines of the climate crisis, such as Monira Bahraldin from Sudan.

She fled El Fasher in wartorn Sudan’s Darfur region in June 2023 and now lives in a refugee settlement in eastern Chad where climate shocks are an ever-present risk, amid ongoing drought and persistent conflict.
“The peak of the dry season in Chad is much hotter than in Darfur, and the journey to fetch water becomes even longer, just as the family’s demand for water increases,” she told the authors.
By 2050, one in three refugee settlements across sub-Saharan Africa could face at least 100 days of dangerous heat each year, according to the report.

Weather-related disasters triggered hundreds of millions of internal displacements worldwide over the past decade, while severe flooding linked to El Niño is expected to force three million people across Somalia, Kenya, South Sudan and Uganda to flee their homes by the end of the year.

Climate change is also making it harder to find lasting solutions for displaced people. More than two-thirds of refugees who returned home in the first half of 2026 went back to countries that are highly vulnerable to climate hazards.

In Syria, meanwhile, nearly four million people have recently returned to the country, where declining groundwater and severe climate shocks are threatening recovery after more than a decade of war. Flooding along the Euphrates River in May damaged homes, displacing thousands once again.

Meanwhile, nearly 90 per cent of stateless people worldwide live in countries that are highly exposed to climate hazards. When climate disasters strike, many struggle to access relief and support, because they lack legal recognition.

The report also shows how refugees and host communities are developing innovative ways to respond to climate change, including solar-powered water systems in the Sahel, climate-resilient agriculture in Uganda and land and mangrove restoration in Colombia.
“Refugees are on the frontlines of the climate crisis, but they are also part of the solution,” Mr. Leis García said.
“COP31 must be a turning point, recognising their leadership and translating bold commitments into concrete investments that reach those most at risk.”

articles.title: Sudan’s suffering is plain for all to see say aid teams, as brutal war continues

paras.en: Sudan’s suffering is plain for all to see say aid teams, as brutal war continues

Aid teams working to help millions of people uprooted by the ongoing war in Sudan appealed on Friday for more international assistance amid desperate funding shortages, empty warehouses and overwhelming needs.

A staggering 15.4 million people urgently require shelter across the country, where war that erupted in April 2023 between former allies turned rival military forces is deepening the suffering of civilians.

“Just yesterday, we had 16 trucks arriving in Darfur, but they were just the last that we had in our stocks. We are facing serious problems. Our supplies are running out,” said Mohamed Refaat, Chief of mission in Sudan for the UN migration agency, IOM, speaking from Khartoum.
Aid access to vulnerable displaced and returning people is better than it was, meaning that “we can reach more people”, the veteran humanitarian officer noted.
But “this means also that we can listen to the stories of their suffering…We cannot say that we don’t know”.

Shifting front lines also continue to force more families to flee their homes, leaving many without anywhere safe to sleep or even a blanket to stay warm, insisted Abubakarr Jalloh, UN refugee agency (UNHCR)’s Deputy Representative in Sudan, speaking via video from Khartoum.

“For a woman who has lost everything, a tent is more than just a shelter; it means the difference between sleeping in the open, surrounded by strangers and having a space of her own. It means dignity. It is privacy. And it is safety for that woman and family.”
For people displaced by conflict, “a solar lamp is more than just a source of light, it is safety,” Mr. Jalloh continued.

“It means a woman can reach a latrine at night without walking in darkness. A kitchen set is also more than a collection of household items. It means a mother can cook for children, without exposing herself to the unnecessary risk.”

In a joint statement issued on Friday, the UN refugee agency (UNHCR) and the International Organization for Migration (IOM) stressed that humanitarian agencies can only assist around one in 10 of those in need because of funding shortages today.

Three in four internally displaced people in Sudan are women and children, Mr. Jalloh said, adding that El Niño-related weather conditions have made people more vulnerable because of significantly below-average rainfall across Sudan this year.

This has affected harvests in Darfur, Kordofan and other areas already devastated by ongoing fighting. Although food prices would normally ease after the harvest season, prices remain “painfully high”, the UNHCR official said.
“For a family that has lost everything, every Sudanese pound spent on food is money that cannot be spent on a blanket or on materials needed for safe shelter,” Mr. Jalloh stressed.

As emergency supplies reaching critically low levels, the UN agencies warned that unless flexible funding is urgently provided, more families will face the coming winter months unprotected from harsh weather conditions, insecurity and the risks of violence and exploitation.
“This year, I was able to distribute more than 40,000 tonnes [of relief assistance]. But our warehouses are completely empty now,” Mr. Refaat said, also speaking via video from Khartoum.
More than 5.2 million people have returned to their areas of origin but many are unable to go back to their homes, as countless numbers have been destroyed or looted.
Healthcare, electricity and water services are also largely unavailable in many locations, meaning that people might be forced to leave again, “without any hope of returning”.

The IOM official also highlighted that Sudanese nationals now constitute the largest nationality arriving in Europe via the so-called Eastern Mediterranean route. “If we are not able to provide aid in Sudan at scale, it means neighbouring countries will be impacted, other countries will be impacted,” he said.

Despite facing the world’s largest displacement crisis, Sudan’s 2026 Humanitarian Needs and Response Plan remains severely underfunded. Only 47 per cent of the required $2.9 billion has been received so far.
Mr. Refaat said that millions of Sudanese families have already lost so much: “We cannot undo what they have endured, but we can make sure that they have a safe place to sleep tonight.”

articles.title: From a ship frozen into Arctic ice, a warning to world leaders: Trust the science

paras.en: From a ship frozen into Arctic ice, a warning to world leaders: Trust the science

Drifting through the polar darkness, a team of scientists is documenting a rapidly changing Arctic. As sea ice retreats and oil tankers move in, a conversation with the UN chief reveals why the battle for climate science matters far beyond the North Pole.
Somewhere in the darkness of the Arctic Ocean, 12 people and a dog named Örkki are drifting right now across the frozen sea, with little say over where they are going.
Their home for the winter is Tara Polar Station, a 26-metre-long French research vessel that departed Norway in August with an unusual purpose: to become trapped in ice.

Locked into a floating sheet of sea ice above more than 2,500 metres of water, the station moves wherever the winds and currents carry it. There is no destination to steer towards, and in the middle of the polar night, no sunlight to mark the passing days.

The team is taking part in Tara Polaris I, the first of 10 planned expeditions in a 20-year international programme to study the transformation of the Arctic Ocean. What they are already witnessing has caught the attention of UN Secretary-General António Guterres.
What happens in the Arctic doesn't stay in the Arctic.

Ahead of the COP31 UN climate conference, the UN chief spoke this week by video link to the expedition’s chief scientist, Maxime Geoffroy, asking what message he should take to world leaders about an Arctic which is warming three to four times faster than the global average.
“I think that, unfortunately, the political leadership in this world is not yet entirely aware of how serious the situation is,” the UN chief said.
Mr. Geoffroy’s message was simple: “What happens in the Arctic doesn't stay in the Arctic.”
The changes unfolding beneath the expedition’s feet could have far-reaching consequences for the world’s oceans, climate and biodiversity, he warned.
The mission draws inspiration from Norwegian explorer Fridtjof Nansen, who famously allowed his vessel to freeze into Arctic sea ice in 1893 and drift with the currents.
More than 130 years later, Mr. Geoffroy and his colleagues are following in his footsteps, with one striking difference: there is considerably less ice in their way.

The expedition spent three weeks navigating along Russia's northern coast before heading into the Arctic ice pack in search of a suitable floe (a large flat piece of floating ice) for its research station.
“We reached 82 degrees north just through leads,” Mr. Geoffroy said, referring to channels of open water between the floes.

When Nansen made his voyage, his vessel became trapped in ice hundreds of kilometres farther south. Now, open stretches of water allowed Mr. Geoffroy's team to travel much deeper before becoming icebound.
But the retreating ice is only part of the story.
The Secretary-General asked Mr. Geoffroy about one of his greatest fears for the future:
“One of the things that has scared me most was the perspective that in a number of years we might have no ice in the Arctic, during summer.”
Arctic sea ice plays a vital role in regulating the Earth’s temperature and keeping the planet cool.
“This large ice sheet on which we are drifting, when the sun comes back, acts as a mirror,” the scientist explained.

Like a giant reflector, the white ice sends much of the Sun’s energy back into space. But as it melts, the darker ocean beneath absorbs that heat instead, warming the water and accelerating the loss of ice.
The consequences are far reaching. Ocean currents carry heat far beyond the North Pole, influencing marine ecosystems and climate patterns across the planet.
As Arctic ice disappears, these circulation systems could be disrupted, with consequences scientists are still struggling to predict.
“We have models, but we don't know when, how, and what will be the exact impacts,” Mr. Geoffroy acknowledged.
The central Arctic remains poorly studied. Firsthand observations are crucial to improving climate models and predicting what lies ahead.
From ancient life to an uncertain future
But the team's questions go far beyond climate forecasts, reaching into one of humanity's oldest mysteries: the origins of life.
Could life on Earth have begun in sea ice?

Mr. Geoffroy pointed to organisms that survive extreme cold thanks to antifreeze proteins, and to the intriguing hypothesis that frozen environments may have played a role in life's earliest beginnings.
Other researchers on board are tackling a more practical mystery: how many fish live in the central Arctic Ocean?
Despite growing commercial interest, researchers still don't know whether its waters could sustain fisheries without threatening fragile ecosystems.
“To understand the loss of biodiversity and protection of biodiversity, you need to know what is there,” the scientist explained.
The research programme brings together 80 scientists and some 220 research protocols to investigate everything from how marine life responds to warming to the ocean’s role in storing carbon.
The Secretary-General, a longstanding advocate for ocean protection, smiled when he heard Mr. Geoffroy describe the international effort as a ‘miniature United Nations for Arctic science’.
But while researchers race to understand the disappearing ice, others are already looking to profit from its retreat.
On their way north, the scientists encountered another unmistakable sign of change: oil tankers navigating the Northeast Passage along Russia’s Arctic coast.
The retreating ice makes the route more accessible but increases the risks of pollution and accidents.
“I can guarantee you that we saw a lot of oil tankers going through that passage,” Mr. Geoffroy told the Secretary-General. “So, it's not just a forecast. It is happening.”
An oil spill in these waters could be disastrous. Petroleum can become trapped in the ice for long periods, threatening marine life and making cleanup exceptionally difficult.

Commercial interests are not the only ones turning their attention north. Guterres pointed to tensions surrounding Greenland and the growing strategic importance of the Arctic, warning that countries increasingly viewing the region through a security lens could threaten the very environment scientists are trying to understand.
For Mr. Geoffroy, whose expedition brings together researchers from 12 countries, the question was whether science could help bridge those geopolitical divides.
“I think that is a central battle we have now. The battle for truth and the battle for science,” the UN chief replied.
The Secretary-General accused powerful economic interests, particularly those linked to fossil fuels, of seeking to obscure scientific evidence and undermine its role in public debate.

“We went from the climate denial to the climate [...] delay and ‘green hushing’,” Mr. Geoffroy observed, lamenting how climate action has slipped down political agendas despite decades of scientific warnings.
Before ending their conversation, the UN chief invited Mr. Geoffroy to imagine addressing world leaders gathering at COP31.
“The findings of this science [...] need to be trusted, they need to be followed and they need to be supported”.
For Guterres, the warning struck a personal chord. He recalled visits to Antarctica and the Himalayas, where he had witnessed glaciers retreating.
Those experiences, combined with the continued refusal of some political leaders to act, had left him with more than concern.
“All these things I think have created in me a sense of urgency and, to be honest, also a sense of fury,” he admitted. “It’s an existential battle,”.
In the Arctic, the researchers will continue their slow drift through the polar darkness, gathering evidence from a region changing before their eyes.

Örkki the dog will keep watch for polar bears while the team measures the ice, water and atmosphere. Thousands of kilometres away, world leaders will gather in Antalya, Türkiye at COP31 to negotiate how to confront the climate crisis.
And while the scientists have no control over where the ice carries them, the future they are documenting remains a matter of human choice.
Follow the latest developments from COP31 through our new podcast, Talk & Action, and our special daily coverage of the conference.

articles.title: Madrid set for 'best in the world' as NFL returns to Spain

paras.en: NFL Madrid: Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor on Joe Burrow, Ja'Marr Chase, Tee Higgins and Bijan Robinson

Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor speaks to Sky Sports NFL as his side prepare to take on the Atlanta Falcons at Real Madrid's Santiago Bernabeu Stadium, live on Sky Sports NFL from 2pm on Sunday.
The 'best passer in the world' might be coming to a Madrid museum near you this weekend. That, of course, is according to Cincinnati Bengals head coach Zac Taylor.
Joe Burrow arrives in Spain as an MVP frontrunner across the first half of the season as his 5-2 Bengals prepare to face the Atlanta Falcons at the Santiago Bernanbeu on Sunday, live on Sky Sports.

Burrow holds a league-high completion percentage of 73 while throwing for 2,115 yards and a league-leading 20 touchdowns to just six interceptions, his 302.1 yards per game also topping all quarterbacks in the NFL.
Cincinnati's poster boy comes into Europe playing some of the football of his life.

"His consistency, and he never wastes a second trying to get himself better," said Taylor, speaking exclusively to Sky Sports, of what makes Burrow special.

"Whether it's his footwork, his placement, reading the body language of the receiver, studying the defense he's going against. He's unbelievable, and he's playing at a high level this year. We're hoping to get that going again on Sunday."
Taylor added in Friday's press conference that Burrow was "arguably the best passer in the world right now".
Between Burrow and a wide receiver tandem of Tee Higgins and Ja'Marr Chase, the Bengals threaten a three-headed monster rivalled by few in the league.

Higgins ranks second in the NFL with 726 receiving yards while Chase has 492 yards, both from 61 targets apiece as two No 1 receivers thriving on the same offense. Together they spearhead the top passing attack in football.

"To have them both on the same team is pretty luxurious for us," said Taylor. "And to be able to put them on the same side, different sides, if defenses are gonna single one of them usually there's great opportunities there for those guys behind them.
"They both have great attention to detail, so we're able to move them around."
On the other side of the ball the Bengals are seeking improvement to a defense that has hindered their Championship credentials in recent seasons.
They sought to addressing as much during the offseason by trading for former New York Giants defensive tackle Dexter Lawrence.
"We got a lot of guys up front that are really talented, Dexter certainly helps us lead the play there," Taylor said.
"He can defend the run and the pass. Teams really have to have a great plan for him in the run and pass game, so he's been a great addition for a lot of things."

Among his prime tasks on Sunday will be slowing down Falcons running back Bijan Robinson, who leads the NFL with 780 rushing yards this season but is without a 100-yard game in Atlanta's last four matchups.
Slowing Robinson is half the battle, such is the foundation he forms for everything Kevin Stefanski wants his offense to be.

"The running back (Robinson) stands out," said Taylor. "He's arguably the best one in the league. You gotta have a great plan. He can go off real quick and then all the things they build off that, the play action, the naked bootlegs, the screens.
"Great on defense, quarterback is great. They do a really good job on that scheme, playing together. And it's gonna make it difficult."
Bengals quarterback Burrow championed the opportunity to play abroad as he explained how this Sunday's game was helping him fulfil a long-term travel dream.

"It means a lot to me that we're here. This is Year 7 for me, and I haven't been overseas yet and we keep adding more and more games to try and build the NFL globally. I think it's worked over the last five years and hoping to add more and continue to build. I love being a part of that and want to help grow the game."
"This is somewhere I've always wanted to go, and so to be able to do it while doing what I love, playing football, really is a dream come true," Burrow said.
Burrow told reporters how he spent time visiting Museo del Prado on Wednesday, with a view to seeing another museum or two and an art gallery before Sunday's game.
Such is the way of an NFL superstar, however, that flying in the radar tends not to be easy, even on European soil
"I ran into some students studying abroad from the United States the other day when I was walking around, that was certainly surprising," Burrow said.

"It's often a little more than I expect when I'm in a different country, I usually expect to go pretty incognito and not have anybody recognise me, it's a little more than that. But I love being out here because I can feel like a normal person a little bit."

articles.title: Ex-NFL receiver Brown avoids prison after pleading guilty to reduced charge

paras.en: Antonio Brown: Ex-NFL wide receiver avoids prison after pleading guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm

Former Pittsburgh Steelers, New England Patriots and Tampa Bay Buccaneers wide receiver Antonio Brown could have faced up to 30 years in prison if convicted of the original attempted murder charge; Brown, 38, says he wants to "get back to life" and his family
Former NFL wide receiver Antonio Brown has avoided jail time after pleading guilty to aggravated assault with a firearm in connection with a 2025 shooting outside a celebrity boxing match Miami.

Judge Marisa Tinkler Mendez sentenced the 38-year-old to three years of probation, during which time he will have to attend weekly counselling sessions and not possess a firearm, among other conditions.
Speaking outside the court, Brown said he wanted to "get back to life" and his family.

His lawyer, Mark Eiglarsh, said: "My client was facing 30 years in prison with a 20-year minimum mandatory, and he was given an offer he just couldn't refuse. Probation was too good to turn down, and we're both very excited about the outcome."

The plea to the reduced charge means the All-Pro wide receiver - who played for the Pittsburgh Steelers from 2010-2018 before spells with the Tampa Bay Buccaneers, where he won the Super Bowl in 2021, and the New England Patriots - has avoided a criminal conviction.

He had had initially been charged with attempted murder after police say he grabbed a handgun from a member of security at the boxing event and fired two shots at a man he had been in a fistfight with earlier.
Brown insisted he was defending himself from an attack as others were trying to steal jewellery from him.
Florida's Stand Your Ground law allows people who believe they face death or serious injury to use deadly force to defend themselves without a duty to retreat.

Prosecutor Howard Rosen said his office was seeking to reduce the charge against Brown because there was "a question" of whether he was actually attempting to shoot the victim, who had been walking away from the altercation at the time.
He noted the victim Zul-Qarnain Kwame Nantambu, who was grazed in the neck, was in court for the hearing and has said publicly that he did not want to press charges.

Rosen said: "Rather than the entire case going away and there being no opportunity for Mr Brown to receive what's ultimately going to be therapeutic treatment, we all came together - the defense and the state - and decided this was in the best interest of everybody."
The victim's lawyer, Richard Cooper, said in a statement: "We are grateful to the court for ratifying this carefully crafted agreement. We have maintained we wish Mr Brown healing."

articles.title: Investors try to regain their footing after tech stocks tank
articles.author: Rob Wile

paras.en: Tech stocks in the U.S. steadied Friday after suffering one of their worst routs in years, as investors weighed the prospect of an AI investment slowdown against future gains following broad Democratic victories in the midterms.
By midday, tech-focused Nasdaq 100 rose 1.9% after plunging 6.3% Thursday, its worst single-day performance since the Covid-19 pandemic.
The broader S&P 500 was nearly 1% higher after tanking 4.4% Thursday, wiping out $2.8 trillion in paper wealth.

Investors continue to digest the results of Tuesday’s midterms that swept a crop of anti-AI and data center opponent politicians into office, including Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa in Texas, among the largest data center markets in the country. The AI boom has comprised an ever-increasing share of stock gains and economic growth writ-large, making markets increasingly susceptible to any threat to the narrative.

“Markets are being punished according to their dependence on the U.S. AI infrastructure cycle,” Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Singapore-based SAXO Markets, told NBC News in emailed comments.

The newly Democrat-controlled Congress could also tighten scrutiny of the industry, including AI infrastructure projects, which could cause delays and additional costs, adding to worries investors have about the profitability of these investments.

Some analysts viewed Thursday’s dramatic sell-off as overblown — or at least, merely a sign of some froth coming off an overstretched market rather than the end of the line for the AI investment wave.

In a note to clients Friday, economist and longtime market watcher Ed Yardeni called recent declines “just speed bumps” that may be helping prevent the AI bubble from over-inflating, and that buying opportunities may already be preventing themselves.
Still, he acknowledged risks remain, namely the extent to which AI data centers get delayed or canceled outright.
Volatility is likely to continue until it becomes clearer how much data center construction is truly threatened by newly elected lawmakers.

“This is a stock market that is trying to figure out the right valuations for the AI trade, which is grappling with a swift sentiment shift after the midterm elections,” Alex Guiliano, chief investment officer at New Jersey-based Resonate Wealth Partners, said in a statement.

Friday kicked off with steep losses in Asia. Japan’s Nikkei suffered its worst week since 2020, falling as much as 6% and more than 20% since its most recent high, putting it in bear-market territory. South Korea’s Kospi index tumbled more than 8%, triggering a temporary market-wide trading halt. There, AI data center memory suppliers Samsung and SK Hynix plunged more than 10% in the early hours, before recovering some of their losses.
In Taiwan, home to some of the most critical AI companies, including chip supplier TSMC, the benchmark TAIEX index dropped 9%.

The companies in Taiwan, South Korea and Japan are linked to the global AI spending cycle and “hence I am not surprised to see the magnitude of correction today following the sharp correction in the U.S.,” Tai Hui, J.P. Morgan’s APAC chief market strategist, told NBC News in emailed comments.

The months leading up to the American elections had already been a rollercoaster for Asian investors, who saw their fortunes soar in June during the AI stock boom, but have been suffering from a brutal recent sell-off.
A sense that valuations of key AI companies were inflated was troublesome enough for markets in Asia, but the Democratic sweep has introduced another layer of uncertainty.
Markets had largely expected losses for Trump’s Republicans, but not on this scale.
“This matters enormously for Asia because much of the hardware supporting America’s AI ambitions is manufactured here,” Chanana, from SAXO Markets, said.
In China, both the tech-focused Star 50 and the AI Index slumped as much as 5% before recouping some losses.
“There is a legitimate argument that parts of China’s AI equity bubble have already burst,” Chanana said.
But she added that unlike the U.S., where much of the investment is commercially driven, “China treats AI and semiconductor self-sufficiency as strategic national priorities.”
“This means investment can continue for reasons beyond immediate profitability, including technological independence, industrial competitiveness and national security.”

That is not the case in South Korea, whose market darlings, memory makers SK Hynix and Samsung, are an integral part of the commercial AI buildout. That makes the country particularly sensitive to any U.S. slowdowns.

South Korea’s benchmark Kospi index more than doubled in market value in June, but by Friday had shed most of the gains made this year. Like South Korea, there is acute exposure for Taiwan — key for advanced chip manufacturing and TSMC’s headquarters.
Nevertheless, most of the Asian indexes are still higher than they were a year ago: South Korea’s Kospi is up 25%, Japan’s Nikkei 225 is up 13%, and TSEC Taiwan Technology is also up by 47%.

“For semiconductor and memory makers in Asia Pacific, as long as global demand for computing power continues to grow, demand for the underlying hardware should remain healthy over the medium term,” J.P. Morgan’s Hui said.
“There may be constraints on where the ‘gold’ can be mined, but as long as demand for the gold remains, the picks and shovels will still be needed elsewhere,” he added.

articles.title: Pope Leo XIV, who had cancer surgery just weeks ago, begins grueling South American tour
articles.author: Claudio Lavanga

paras.en: ABOARD THE PAPAL FLIGHT — Three countries in 12 days, a dozen flights, two helicopter rides and nine Masses on a trip covering around 19,000 miles. Less than a month after Pope Leo XIV underwent cancer surgery, he set off on what the Vatican called a “homecoming” tour of South America.
The 71-year-old’s long trip across the strongly Catholic region will take him to Uruguay and Argentina, as well as to Peru, where he lived for decades and served as a bishop until 2023.

Leo considers the tour, one of the most grueling undertaken by a Catholic leader in decades, a “homecoming to places where he spent a long time and to which he feels closely connected,” Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni told journalists at a briefing Tuesday.

The Chicago-born pontiff, who is also a citizen of Peru, told pilgrims at his weekly audience in St. Peter’s Square on Wednesday that he was hoping to “strengthen the faith, renew hope” and “rekindle the fire of charity.”
Leo will hold several meetings with survivors of sexual abuse by Catholic clergy during the trip, the Vatican has said, without yet providing further details.

Bruni said the pope would also address a range of issues facing the continent, including environmental destruction, arms trafficking and regional political instability, bringing “a message of communion and unity.”
Leo departed from Rome’s Fiumicino Airport early Friday, and is due to arrive in Uruguay at 4:30 p.m. local time (2:30 p.m. ET) for the country’s first papal visit since 1988.

Considered the most secular country in the region, where only a fraction of people go to Mass regularly, Uruguay was the first in the world to legalize marijuana for recreational use and the second country in Latin America to decriminalize abortion.
In October 2025, the country of just 3.5 million people became the first in the region to approve legislation for assisted dying despite strong opposition from the Catholic Church.
After Uruguay, Leo’s tour will take him to Argentina for three days, where he is expected to meet with right-wing President Javier Milei, a close ally of President Donald Trump.
It will be the first papal visit to Argentina since Pope John Paul II traveled to the country in 1987.
Leo’s immediate predecessor, Pope Francis, was born in Argentina, the first pontiff from the region, but he declined numerous invitations to return to his homeland.

The biggest crowds of the trip are likely next week during his six-day visit to Peru, where Leo is widely celebrated as a beloved national figure. He will stop off in the capital, Lima, before visiting his former diocese of Chiclayo, where he was ordained bishop in 2014 and remained until taking up a Vatican post in 2023.
Leo, who was treated last month for lung adenocarcinoma, the most common form of lung cancer, will also make several high-altitude visits in the Peruvian Andes.

Doctors have said that the disease was localized and that he would not require any further treatments; Bruni said Leo had recovered enough that no additional medical measures would be necessary during his trip.

Speaking at the same briefing Tuesday, Maria Montserrat Alvarado, the Vatican’s new communications chief, said Leo was grateful for the concern about his health and the demands the journey might make on him.
But, she said, he was “so excited” to make the trip.

articles.title: Meghan Markle’s father arrested in Florida over alleged child sexual abuse material
articles.author: Nick Duffy

paras.en: Thomas Markle, the estranged father of Meghan, the Duchess of Sussex, was arrested in Florida on Friday over allegations he possessed child sexual abuse material, including sexually explicit photographs of himself with minors, the Justice Department announced.
He is charged with one count of possession of child pornography, according to a criminal complaint.

The FBI seized around 78 items from two storage units rented by Markle that contain “suspected child pornography,” according to court documents. Items seized include film negatives featuring an adult man with naked “pre-pubescent” girls, and a witness “positively identified the adult man as Markle,” according to the documents.
Markle, 82, is expected to make his initial appearance Friday in the U.S. District Court for the Middle District of Florida in Tampa, the Justice Department said.
“These allegations are extremely serious, and we will prosecute Mr. Markle to the fullest extent of federal law,” First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said in a statement.
“Working with our Justice Department partners, our agents moved quickly, identified and located the explicit material, and arrested Mr. Markle in Florida,” FBI Director Kash Patel said.

His arrest comes weeks after authorities in the Philippines said they were investigating allegations that he kept child sexual abuse images at his home while living there. Authorities in the country later said they had recovered thousands of photos featuring “underage male and females.”
Markle, a retired television lighting and photography director, denied the allegations last month, calling them “sick lies.”
A spokesperson for the Prince Harry and Meghan, the Duke and Duchess of Sussex, declined to comment on the arrest. Buckingham Palace has not responded to a request for comment.

In a criminal complaint, the FBI said Markle had rented the two storage units in California since the summer of 2008. One unit had mail bearing the name Thomas Markle and an international driver’s permit with his name, birthdate and a photo appearing to be him.
The FBI seized 27 items from one unit and 51 from the other. Some of the film negatives, books and slides seized from them still are being reviewed.

At least 18 images made from converted negatives “appeared to constitute child pornography,” according to the complaint. At least two images involved an adult, clothed man and a nude female child, the complaint states. A witness identified the man in the images as Markle, the FBI said.

The FBI determined some of the seized film was manufactured in New York, so it would have traveled to California as interstate commerce. Based on background in one photo, the FBI determined the images were taken in a hotel in the Philippines, according to the court document.

Meghan said in a statement last month that she was “deeply distressed” by the allegations against her father. Their relationship has been limited and fraught in recent years, with her father not attending her wedding to Harry in 2018 amid widespread media scrutiny.

Her statement said that she was previously informed of “disturbing allegations” against him, with British police subsequently confirming she was passed a letter in January 2019 “containing a number of claims about alleged offending outside the United Kingdom.”

London’s Metropolitan Police force said it had not informed other law enforcement agencies about the allegations in the letter at the time, referring itself to Britain’s policing watchdog over the handling of the allegations.

“The breadth of what has now been uncovered is more sickening than one could ever imagine,” said Meghan, who said she had chosen to keep her children, Prince Archie, 7, and Princess Lilibet, 5, away from her father “for one reason: to protect them.”
Harry and Meghan stepped back as working royals in 2020 amid widespread reports of a royal rift, leaving Britain for California.
Harry, the second son of King Charles and late Princess Diana, leveled harsh criticism at Buckingham Palace and other senior royals across a series of media interviews and a tell-all memoir, “Spare.”
The couple returned to Britain two months ago, with their two children moving to schools in the country.

articles.title: Convicted rapist Brand facing at least four more investigations

paras.en: If Russell Brand was at all worried about being found guilty in his four-week rape and sexual assault trial, he was not showing it.
I was standing a few people behind the British actor and comedian in the queue for security checks outside London's Southwark Crown Court on Wednesday, when he broke briefly into song.
"Sweet Caroline," he sang to a woman beside him in the line, quoting the famous Neil Diamond hit.
The woman had introduced herself to the star as Caroline, and the pair chatted jovially while waiting to move forward.
Inside court, just minutes later, the jury began its second day of deliberations.
On other mornings, as Brand was greeted at court by a flurry of camera flashes, journalists asked how he was feeling.
Throughout the trial, the comedian-turned-born-again Christian influencer continued to make social media videos with his wife, Laura, for their millions of followers.
As the court heard harrowing, graphic and often tearful accounts from Brand's six accusers, he did not flinch.
When he gave evidence himself, he did so standing up unnaturally straight.
At crunch time — when the guilty verdicts were read out on Thursday — the comedian stood to attention like a soldier on parade and showed no emotion.
When his lawyer applied for bail ahead of sentencing on Monday, he said his client wanted time to say goodbye to his wife and three children over the weekend.
Outside court and in, this was a defendant who did not seem to think he would go to jail.
Brand has been on trial since mid-October for seven historical sex offences relating to six women spanning a decade from 1999 to 2009.
After eight and a half hours of deliberations, the jury of four women and eight men found him guilty of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault.
He was acquitted of a further two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.
On the steps of Southwark Crown Court afterwards, police praised the "extraordinary courage, resilience and determination" of the women, while pulling no punches about Brand.

"Russell Brand used his influence, status, and fame to prey on and exploit women. As his profile grew, so too did his sense of entitlement," Detective Superintendent Andy Furphy, from London's Metropolitan Police Service, said.
"I hope this conviction sends a clear message that no one is above the law, no matter how famous or powerful they may be."

During the trial, journalists could only report what was said and done in front of the jury, but with verdicts returned and restrictions lifted, we can now give more detail from one of the most high-profile criminal trials in recent British history.
Brand is no longer a mainstream comedian and actor, and instead styles himself as a Christian influencer, broadcasting online prayer videos and sermons to millions.
His faith was on full public display from day one of the trial. When he was first shown into the dock before jury selection, he went down on one knee and appeared to pray.
During the trial he wore crucifixes of different sizes, he sometimes carried a bible with sticky notes marking pages, and at least one day he was handling what looked like prayer beads.
Unusually for a defendant in a criminal trial, he posted repeatedly on social media — not about the evidence but about his feelings, his faith, and his disdain for the mainstream media.
It can now be reported that Brand's legal team tried to have the case thrown out, before the trial had even begun because of negative press about him.

Barrister Ian Winter KC argued his client could not receive a fair trial because of 2023 media reports with allegations about Brand — allegations that prompted the women who would ultimately be the complainants in this trial to come forward.
Mr Winter's application was denied, but he would go on to say during the trial that the 2023 reporting had "poisoned the well".
The 2023 allegations in the media were not part of the trial.
In an extraordinary moment in the corridor at the end of proceedings, Mr Winter launched a tirade at Sunday Times Chief News Correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who worked on the 2023 investigation.
“I hope you are pleased with yourself,” Mr Winter said.
Ms Urwin responded that she was “pleased justice has been done".
Mr Winter replied, “well, it wasn’t. You f***** it. Congratulations".
On Friday the top silk reported himself to the Bar Standards Board over the exchange.
There were other moments of courtroom drama during the trial.

On day one, lawyers for People Magazine in the US were hauled before Judge Joel Bennathan to explain why the magazine had reported the attempt to have the case thrown out, when a court order had been made to keep that out of the public domain.
Judge Bennathan then put journalists in court and beyond on notice that he would not be lenient if there were further contempt of court risks.
Another day, police arrested a blogger who had identified one of Brand's accusers, all of whom are granted lifelong anonymity by the court.
The man, who had been sitting in the spillover court watching proceedings on a large video screen, was detained for 12 hours, cautioned, and forced to amend his blog posts.
Police appeal for other women to come forward
There are more allegations about Brand that we can now report too.

The Metropolitan Police revealed its detectives are currently investigating allegations of rape from two more women in the UK, while there are two civil claims afoot against Brand relating to his time in the US.
The head of Scotland Yard Sir Mark Rowley has said he "wouldn't be surprised" if more people came forward to make allegations. He has appealed for them to do so.
Brand, meanwhile, is spending his first weekend behind bars.
Judge Bennathan denied his bail application saying that while he regrets the impact on the 51-year-old's children, their father had the resources to be a flight risk.
"I think there are substantial grounds to fear he might in the end not feel able to come along and face his sentence,"
The verdict marks a massive fall from grace for the entertainer; once a swaggering exhibitionist performing to huge crowds, now a convicted rapist in a prison cell.
For the rape and three sexual assaults he was found guilty of this week, Brand will be sentenced on Monday.
The judge has already flagged the rape conviction alone will mean a "significant custodial sentence".

articles.title: Breaking: Trump to replace chief of staff with hardline deputy Stephen Miller
articles.author: Riley Stuart

paras.en: Donald Trump has announced that his chief of staff Susie Wiles will be replaced by her hardline deputy Stephen Miller on Monday.
The US President made the announcement on Friday, local time, in a social media post.
Mr Trump thanked Ms Wiles for doing an "outstanding job" and said she would move to a different role in his "political operation".
In reality, the switch sidelines one of his most senior staff members.
"I want to thank her for her service as chief of staff," Mr Trump's post read. "She has done a great job!"
Analysts have widely speculated Mr Trump will reshuffle his administration after his Republican Party's disastrous performance at this week's midterm elections.
In March, Ms Wiles announced she would be taking time away from her role after being diagnosed with breast cancer.
Mr Miller is best-known as the architect of the Trump administration's immigration crackdown.
The 41-year-old has long been involved in shaping immigration policy in the GOP.
He was Mr Trump's chief immigration advisor during the president's first term.
Before that, Mr Miller worked for Senator Jeff Sessions, who was renowned as one of the chamber's loudest and most uncompromising voices on the subject.

Most recently, Mr Miller has driven the push for mass deportations, pressing ICE leadership to raise arrest numbers and publicly telling officers they would have "federal immunity in the conduct of your duties".

articles.title: Endangered crayfish return home months after Victorian bushfires
articles.author: Erin Somerville and Andrew Mangelsdorf

paras.en: An endangered crayfish species was rescued after bushfires in January tore through Victoria's High Country.
Some are now returning home after months in captivity.
Conservationists expect more species will need rescuing after bushfires amid climate change.
In a rugged corner of Victoria's High Country, two scientists are making their way slowly through fire-scarred bushland that is slowly returning to life.
They are travelling with precious cargo: a group of endangered alpine spiny crayfish that are heading back to their home waterway near Lucyvale.

The scientists were here in the immediate aftermath of the January bushfires that tore through the region, and they salvaged 11 endangered crayfish that were at risk of suffocating in the stream from debris and sediment.

The alpine spiny crayfish are restricted in their movement and found in small, isolated pockets that make it tricky for scientists to find, adding to the pressure of rescue efforts as water quality declines after a fire.
"If they aren't rescued they can disappear from these areas," Arthur Rylah Institute senior scientist Will Sowersby said.

The alpine spiny crayfish were taken to the Snobs Creek conservation hatchery, which is run by the Victorian Fisheries Authority near Eildon, where they were cared for until water quality improved post-bushfires.
It is the first time the endangered species has been taken into captivity, and it proved a learning curve for staff.
"It's a new process for us," Snobs Creek's senior conservation hatchery officer Dylan White said.
"They are a bit feisty so we have had to separate them, and we have kept them separate this whole time because they will attack each other."

As the Victorian High Country starts to spring back to life from the Walwa-River Road bushfire that burnt around 121,000 hectares, scientists are continuing to monitor the alpine spiny crayfish's habitat and ponder their future.
Conservationists hope the endangered crayfish can be included in a future captive breeding program at the Snobs Creek hatchery to help bolster numbers and geographical diversity.
But with another summer on the horizon, Mr Sowersby predicts their work is far from over.

"We know that bushfires are increasing in their frequency and their intensity, so we suspect it's going to be more and more important that we rescue species post-bushfire and that we also establish new populations to (prevent) the risk of an extinction event due to a catastrophic fire," he said.
It has been a busy year for Snobs Creek hatchery staff who carry out important conservation work with vulnerable species, especially after natural disasters.
"Most of these species we have here are so critically endangered they have never been kept in captivity before, so it's really new for everyone," Mr White said.
"The important thing is we are experienced and we are putting that knowledge and skill set towards caring for them and learning more about them."
Some of the species at the facility are found nowhere else in the world.

That includes a special type of galaxias fish that only exists in a sole tributary of the La Trobe River after experiencing a major population collapse in the past decade, and the critically endangered blackfish that were rescued after bushfires tore through the Grampians region.
Some species rescued after Victoria's summer bushfires have already been re-released, including more than 100 Macquarie perch and trout cod taken from Seven Creek after the Longwood bushfire.
"It was quite challenging to look after a large number of trout cod at the same time due to their aggressive nature …took up a lot of space," Snobs Creek head of fish production Chris Mullins said.
The species' stay at the facility can be hard work for staff, who have to manage unique diets, water temperature, lighting, and behavioural issues.
With Australia predicted to face more natural disaster as climate change progresses, staff value the significance of the hatchery.
"Every year (natural disasters) seems to be getting more and more, so we have got to have a facility here that we can take some of these species as quickly as we can," Mr White said.
"If we weren't doing it no one would be."

articles.title: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
articles.author: Sara Jabakhanji

paras.en: What we know about Europe's latest wave of bomb threats targeting flights — and now newsrooms
It's not clear if all threats are linked

A spate of bomb threats across Europe has thrown airports and newsrooms into disarray over the past week, forcing flight diversions and emergency landings while prompting broadcast suspensions and evacuations to conduct security sweeps.

No explosives have been found, and the threats have so far proved unfounded. But the spate of hoaxes that affected a number of flights, airports and, as of Friday, news broadcasters has raised concern over the widening impact if the threats continue to spread.

It's not yet clear if the incidents are linked, but the bomb threat hoaxes come on the heels of other European disruptions, including attacks on supermarket refrigeration systems and drone incursions.
Here is what we know about the hoaxes targeting airlines and broadcasters in Europe.
What appeared to be a co-ordinated wave of bomb threats targeting European air traffic began on Tuesday.

At least seven flights and a cruise ship received hoax bomb threats, triggering emergency landings, fighter jet escorts and temporary airport closures in countries including Poland, Bulgaria, Italy and Spain.
A second wave was reported on Thursday, with at least 27 flights affected.

On Friday, Prague's Vaclav Havel Airport said a total of nine flights were threatened, including arriving flights from Denmark, Spain and Britain, and departing flights to the Netherlands, Cyprus, Romania, Italy and Britain.

Newsrooms in Ireland and Bulgaria received emailed bomb threats on Friday from a purported "Mikhail Andropov" claiming responsibility for a widening wave of hoax threats disrupting passenger flights across Europe.

The messages, sent to Bulgaria's Nova TV and the Irish public broadcaster RTE, which evacuated its offices and suspended programming, were headlined "Message to the West" and portrayed the threats as the prelude to a series of attacks on means of transport across Europe.
The British broadcaster Sky also said it had received a security threat.

Reuters was not able to establish the identity of the sender, the origin of the emails or whether they had in fact come from the same source as the threats to any or all of the dozens of flights affected since Tuesday.

Garda members work outside the offices of Irish National broadcaster RTE on Friday after staff were evacuated from the site following a bomb threat. The broadcaster has claimed the bomb threat is from the same group that has been behind a wave of bomb threats issued to passenger flights around Europe this week. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)

Bomb threats against planes are often communicated to airlines, airports or authorities through anonymous emails or phone calls claiming that an explosive device is on board. Authorities do not always disclose how threats are delivered, because doing so could encourage copycats and compromise investigations.

A Prague airport representative told CNN on Thursday that they had received a threat from an anonymous email addressed to the airport, and Czech police said similar emails went to other European airports.

Eric Schouten, head of aviation security group Dyami, told Reuters that an airline's security department first runs the report through a checklist. It then alerts the authorities, who may scramble fighter jets or divert the plane to a designated airport for a full sweep.
The vast majority of bomb threats turn out to be false alarms, though all must be treated as real until investigated, which means authorities are forced to scramble to rule out any danger.
No explosive device has been found on the planes affected this week, but every airline must decide whether a threat is credible and act accordingly.
A spokesperson for the British government called this week's incidents "malicious hoax threats" and said it has "one of the most robust aviation security systems in the world."
- String of bomb threats on flights, cruise ship disrupt travel across Europe
- Bomb threats affect at least 27 flights, leading to emergency landings at several European airports
Airlines are not new to bomb threats, but aviation security experts say the apparent co-ordination and timing of the current incidents is unusual.
All planes, including those threatened on Friday, landed safely.
Authorities have not attributed the threats to any group or state actor, and no evidence has emerged linking the hoaxes to a government.

The incidents come at a time when many European officials have accused Russia of a campaign of "hybrid" or "grey zone" disruptions that are essentially cheap to execute, easy to deny and not expected to trigger an armed response.
Countries affected by the disruptions, including Denmark, Poland and Romania, have previously accused Moscow. Russia denies any involvement.
An EasyJet aircraft takes off at Vaclav Havel Airport in Prague. (David W. Cerny/Reuters)

On Thursday, an airport source in Italy said bomb threats had been sent to several airlines and airport operators in Rome and Milan purporting to be from "fighters of the Male State," a far-right anti-feminist movement banned in Russia.
Reuters could not confirm who had sent the email. Vladislav Pozdnyakov, a Russian blogger who set up Male State in 2016, said it no longer existed and was not involved in any way.

Rhys Jones, analysis output manager at aviation risk advisory firm Osprey Flight Solutions, said bomb threats can stem from a wide range of motives, including political grievances, activist campaigns, criminal activity, online groups or state-linked hybrid operations.

European technology commissioner Henna Virkkunen says that since 2022, Europe had faced a range of hybrid operations, including sabotage of critical infrastructure, drone incursions, cyber breaches and election interference.
“We are under attack all the time,” she told Reuters. “The reason behind these operations is to destabilize our societies and create mistrust among our citizens.”
“It’s not always Russia who is behind different hybrid operations. Quite often, it is Russia.”
Overall, the threats have caused minimal disruption to aviation, according to Eurocontrol, the European air traffic authority.

Even a false alarm can disrupt airlines' operations, with plane diversions and thorough security inspections causing delays for passengers. Carriers typically bear additional costs including fuel, passenger rebooking, crew disruption and aircraft diversions.
Schouten said a sweep means unloading passengers and baggage, searching the aircraft and reloading. That can push crews past duty limits and lead to missed connections and cancellations.
People gather outside the offices of Irish national broadcaster RTE as officials conduct a security sweep after a reported bomb threat on Friday. (Natalia Campos/Reuters)
Air France-KLM chief executive Ben Smith said on Thursday he had never previously seen threats reported in such a co-ordinated fashion.

"We're quite confident that we have in place what we need to ensure that it has minimal or no impact on our operation," Smith told reporters. "So we have no ask today of our governments to change the way they manage these types of situations."
Which airlines, airports have been affected?
Bomb threats are on pilots' minds and create unnecessary tension, but crews are prepared to respond professionally, said Paul Reuter, vice-president of the European Cockpit Association.
Pilots review procedures with cabin crews, identify airports where they could divert and may carry extra fuel, he said.
Reuter called the use of civil aviation for geopolitical disruption or hoaxes "totally unacceptable."
With files from Reuters and The Associated Press

articles.title: Trump's Justice Department hit by 2 high-profile departures this week

paras.en: Trump's Justice Department hit by 2 high-profile departures this week
Jason Reding Quiñones, Harmeet Dhillon, who each led controversial probes, leaving administration

Jason Reding Quiñones, who oversaw probes into past criminal investigations of U.S. President Donald Trump as the top federal prosecutor in Miami, has resigned, Attorney General Todd Blanche said on Friday.
“We are grateful for Jason’s leadership in combating violent crime, drug trafficking, sex trafficking, and transnational crime,” said Blanche.
It was not immediately clear why Quiñones resigned. In a statement on X, Quiñones said his resignation was effective Friday and called it an honour to serve in the role.

His office has been involved in investigations related to the 2021 assassination of Haitian President Jovenel Moïse, and had also brought criminal charges against former Cuban president Raúl Castro in a major escalation of the Trump administration's pressure campaign against the communist country.
- Analysis JD Vance blames Iran war for midterm thumping. Is he really blaming Trump?
- Analysis Ohio and Texas went from red to blue in the midterms but may not stay that way in 2028
As U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Florida, Quiñones was at the centre of Trump's attempts to leverage the Justice Department to exact revenge on his political adversaries.
The investigation, which officials dubbed a “grand conspiracy," sought to establish that the president was the victim of a long-running criminal conspiracy.

The office was tasked with investigating whether officials in the Barack Obama and Joe Biden administrations had engaged in criminal conduct while overseeing probes of Trump's handling of classified documents after he left office in 2021 as well as his campaign's contacts with Russia in the 2016 election, among other issues.
Former CIA director John Brennan and former FBI agents were among those subpoenaed to answer questions as part of the probes.

The efforts have not led to any charges being filed. Lawyers Joseph DiGenova and Kurt Olsen, who each supported Trump as he sought to prevent his 2020 presidential election defeat, had joined the team based in Florida but announced their resignations in recent weeks.
Dhillon 'decimated' civil rights unit: critic
On Thursday, Harmeet Dhillon, who reshaped the Justice Department's civil rights unit to pursue Trump administration priorities including voter data requests and gun rights cases, also resigned.

Leading into this week's midterms, in which Democrats flipped many Republican seats to win back control of Congress, Dhillon led an effort to obtain voter rolls from about 30 U.S. states, most of them with Democratic leadership. Those lawsuits were rejected 27 times by the courts, with a federal judge in a California voter roll case calling them "unprecedented and illegal."
The efforts were motivated by a belief from the Trump administration that the voter list was filled with noncitizens.
Harmeet Dhillon is shown at a news conference in Washington on Aug. 7, 2025. (Jose Luis Magana/The Associated Press)

Dhillon also led investigations to pressure dozens of universities she viewed as too liberal. Many of those centred on alleged antisemitism, diversity initiatives, and treatment of transgender people. Those probes helped the department extract hundreds of millions of dollars in settlement agreements from some of the nation’s premier universities but one high-profile target, Harvard University, refused to pay a large settlement and instead has repeatedly fought the Trump administration in court.

“We ushered in the downfall of illegal DEI, we fought to protect women and girls’ sports, and so much more,” Dhillon said in a social media post announcing her departure, using the acronym for diversity, equity and inclusion. Dhillon, a Sikh born in India to parents who immigrated to the U.S. when she was a child, is expected to return to her private law firm.
The civil rights unit also brought a case against former CNN anchor Don Lemon and others who were protesting in a church over the Trump administration’s immigration crackdown in Minnesota.

The civil rights division in prior administrations conducted investigations into police departments accused of systematic civil rights violations, including after high-profile killings of Black people by local police. Under Dhillon, police reform settlements brought about after the police killings of George Floyd and Breonna Taylor were scrapped.
More than three quarters of the unit’s workforce at the beginning of Trump’s second term have left.

"For almost 70 years, the Civil Rights Division brought to fruition the civil rights laws that Americans demanded. Dhillon decimated it," said Stacey Young, a former Justice Department official who now heads Justice Connection, an advocacy group.
- John Bolton, former Trump adviser, pleads guilty to 1 count of illegally retaining classified info
- Video Midterms ‘bluenami’: The exact moment Trump lost control of Congress | About That
Blanche on Friday also announced the resignation of a less visible figure in the department, John Eisenberg, assistant attorney general for the national security division.

Eisenberg was involved in the prosecution of former national security adviser John Bolton, according to a Politico report. Bolton, a former Trump administration official often criticized by the president, is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to a count of illegally retaining classified information.

Both Eisenberg and Bolton in Trump's first term refused requests to appear before Democratic committees investigating a controversial phone call between the U.S. president and Ukraine President Volodymyr Zelenskyy. Trump was impeached by the House of Representatives on charges of abuse of power and obstruction of Congress, but later acquitted in the Senate.
With files from CBC News and the Associated Press

articles.title: Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida Learjet crash says final radio calls showed 'she's tough'

paras.en: Dad of 20-year-old co-pilot in Florida Learjet crash says final radio calls showed 'she's tough'
Family held news conference to push back against online criticism over her age, experience

The father of the 20-year-old co-pilot who died along with eight others when their Learjet crashed in Florida said Friday he has listened to his daughter's heartbreaking final radio transmissions "many times" since the crash.

Allan Filgueiras, himself a pilot, was searching for answers as to why the plane plunged from the sky on Sunday — but what he found was immense pride in how his daughter, Nathalia Gadelha Filgueiras, handled the crisis.
"I did listen to that many times trying to find a clue. In my head. How'd that happen? And wow, she's tough," Allan Filgueiras said at a news conference Friday, frequently holding back tears.

In her final conversation with air traffic control, she can be heard calmly reporting ice buildup on the plane as the Learjet flew into a thunderstorm and turbulence tossed it up and down by 200 metres. The situation quickly escalated as the aircraft fell at breathtaking speed. "Declare an emergency 722-Bravo-Delta. We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute!" she said.
Her father and aviation safety experts have been impressed that Filgueiras continued to call out updates on what was happening even as she realized the plane's fate was sealed.
"For the family — it's like having the heart torn from my chest," her father said in Spanish. "I have to find a way to go on living."

The family wants to push back against online criticism over whether she had enough experience to be in the cockpit of a Learjet. She had more than 1,300 hours of experience and completed extensive training to earn her commercial pilot's licence.
So her father held Friday's news conference, which his lawyer said was designed to "preserve not just her memory, but her reputation."

"She was at the top of her class in everything that she did, and she was perfectly qualified to be the co-pilot on this flight, despite her tender years," attorney Stuart Grossman said, noting there were no immediate plans to file a lawsuit over the crash.

It's far too early in the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation to know what caused the crash. As it fell, the Learjet accelerated beyond its design limits and pieces of the plane's tail were found kilometres away from the crash site.

Retired airline pilot John Cox, who is now the CEO of Safety Operating Systems, said he started out flying professionally at age 19, meaning he was in the same situation as Filgueiras when he started his career. He said she was doing quite well to earn the co-pilot's seat she had.
"To be in the right seat of a Lear 60, she had to impress somebody, because that's a good ride. I mean, that's great. I know she loved it," Cox said.
Her father believes she held up in the midst of a crisis better than most.

"She showed me what it is to be a hero because once you see that coming, a lot of the big boys — military or whatever — they can't handle. And she was the one over there to the last minute fighting," Allan Filgueiras said.

The victims included technology entrepreneur Adam Robinson; his wife, Helen Sharp; and their two young children, relatives said. The family's nanny, Ana María Ramírez Cetina, was also killed. The plane's captain, who was pilot in command as the plane fell, was 55-year-old Jeff Gregory.

articles.title: Czech arms makers set sights on space defense in bid to sustain Ukraine-driven arms boom

paras.en: The Czechoslovak Group (CSG) arms maker announced in mid-October that it has acquired a stake in Canadian space technology manufacturer MDA Space.
This space mission is part of the company's bid to continue riding the boom that has transformed its fortunes in recent years.

When it listed on the Amsterdam Stock Exchange earlier this year, CSG soared to become the most valuable company in Central and Eastern Europe, with a market capitalization of €14.6 billion ($16.4 billion), propelling its owner, Michal Strnad, to the top of the region's rich list.
From 90s startup to major European player

CSG began life as a 1990s startup, selling military surplus amid the collapse of the Warsaw Pact, the military alliance between the Soviet Union and Europe's socialist Eastern Bloc nations, which was founded in 1955 and disbanded in 1991.
It has since grown to become the second-largest producer of ammunition in Europe after Germany's Rheinmetall and now produces across Europe and in the US.
The main driver of the company's rising fortunes has been Russia's war in Ukraine, which has driven a dramatic boom across the Czech defense industry as a whole.
In 2021, the sector's exports totaled €600 million. In 2025, these exports had expanded to €4.7 billion, powered by orders placed by Kyiv and its European allies.
By the end of that year, European states had procured approximately €11 billion worth of military support for Ukraine from Czech defense firms.
Orders to the value of roughly €4 billion have arrived via the Czech Ammunition Initiative, a program that coordinates the transfer of artillery shells to Ukraine.

Amid the avalanche of orders sparked by Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, CSG and Czech peers such as STV, Colt CZ and PBS have been busy expanding production to pump out military vehicles and planes, guns, grenades, shells and bullets.
"The war in Ukraine, particularly in its early stages, was especially well suited to Czech firms," Krzysytof Debiec of the Centre for Eastern Studies (OSW) told DW.
Debiec says that this was largely due to the major role that the former Czechoslovakia played in supplying Warsaw Pact countries.

"Specialization in the production of ammunition — including Soviet calibers — the repair of Soviet-era equipment and the manufacture of relatively unsophisticated systems that could be rapidly introduced and were compatible with the Ukrainian army's existing stocks," have all been key, he explained.
At the same time, European states eyeing the threat from the east and broader geopolitical instability are boosting their own defense budgets.

"The shift in US policies vis-a-vis NATO is forcing European nations to increase their defense spending dramatically, and that's another factor" in the Czech defense industry boom, Jan Jires, a former deputy defense minister and now a senior advisor at the International Institute for Strategic Studies, told DW.
However, since launching on the stock exchange, CSG's share price has performed erratically, illustrating the shifting sands on which Czechia's booming defense industry now stands.

The government in Prague has responded to the sector's surge by transferring the defense industry portfolio from the Ministry of Defense to the Ministry of Industry and Trade to align its growing role in exports with national economic and trade policy.

At the same time, the populist ruling coalition that took power a year ago is made up of parties that have either promised to lower support for Ukraine or — in the case of the far-right Freedom and Direct Democracy party (SPD) — are openly pro-Russian.
As a result, the coalition has halted contributions to the Czech Ammunition Initiative and is dragging its feet on raising defense spending to meet NATO targets.

This only limits an already small domestic market, leaving the industry dependent on exports for about 90% of its revenue — the vast bulk of which is still linked to Ukraine — and lacking a stable base for expansion.

"The Czech industry has outgrown the country's financial means," said Jires. "Unlike German, French or British companies, Czech manufacturers cannot rely on domestic demand to make them globally relevant."

Increased global defense spending looks set to continue, but an end to Russia's war in Ukraine, a change in US foreign policy or a calmer geopolitical environment would hit Czech arms manufacturers hard. For this reason, they must ponder what the future of war, and its funding, might look like.

The conflict in Ukraine offers some indicators, having become increasingly focused on swarms of drones and a technological race between Kyiv and Moscow to improve the performance of the unmanned aircraft.

Major questions must now be asked regarding "the size and role of the military, how it is equipped, what should be purchased and when new weaponry can arrive" Andor Sandor, a defense analyst and former commander of Czechia's Military Intelligence Service, told DW.
For a company like CSG, for which bullets and shells currently account for around 60% of sales, these are vital questions.

"Czech companies — many of which still focus on relatively unsophisticated military production — must invest more in innovative manufacturing," said Debiec, who notes that most are well aware of the challenge. "They have reinvested their extraordinary profits and are already more technologically advanced and diversified in their production than they were in 2022."
CSG's acquisition of MDA Space is part of such efforts.
The company, which already held interests in British and German space technology companies, pointed to the close link between the space and defense industries when it announced the deal.

Noting that global government spending on space defense accelerated to €65.83 billion last year, CSG estimates that the overall space economy will triple in size to €1.6 trillion over the next decade.
Developing capabilities in space is "a natural extension" of its activities, the company stated, noting plans for further development in the segment, including a "dedicated space team."

To power such missions, Czech defense companies must make sure they're in a position to tap into funds for defense and space under the next EU budget, which could rise as high as €130 billion, said Jires.
"If they fail to do so, and all this money is grabbed by German, French and Italian companies," he warned, "Czech manufacturers may miss the opportunity to truly scale-up."

articles.title: Protests and reforms: France's rising debt costs threaten stability

paras.en: Deeply indebted, politically trapped in a standoff between extremes and led by a government without a parliamentary majority: These are the defining features of France's current predicament.

If, in response to nationwide protests, the government plans to provide €4 billion ($4.48 billion) in low-interest loans to renovate schools by 2030 and allocate a further €1 billion to universities by 2029, it is promising money the state simply does not have.

France's public debt stands at around 120% of gross domestic product (GDP). By comparison, Germany's debt-to-GDP ratio is roughly 65%, despite its €600 billion investment package for infrastructure and defense.

Germany still enjoys the highest possible AAA credit rating. France, by contrast, is rated AA, A+ or Aa3, depending on the credit agency. While Germany's outlook is consistently rated as stable, several agencies have assigned France a negative outlook.

As a result, the French government must pay higher interest rates on its borrowing than Berlin. The risk premium over German government bonds, known as the spread, is now at its highest level since the financial crisis. France pays nearly 1.6 percentage points more in interest than Germany on 10-year bonds.
The spread acts as a kind of fever gauge for bond markets, explains Friedrich Heinemann, an economist at the Leibniz Center for European Economic Research (ZEW) in Mannheim.

"This fever gauge then forces a change of course. If the spread rises too sharply, France's financing conditions come under pressure, and anyone in France who needs a loan has to pay higher interest rates. Banks then get into trouble, and the crisis escalates further," Heinemann told DW.

"This could then slide towards a financial crisis, which would finally send a clear signal to everyone: Things cannot continue like this unless you are prepared to risk a genuine economic collapse," he explained.

Landry Charrier, a researcher at the University of Bonn's Center for Advanced Security, Strategic and Integration Studies, however, does not expect France's debt-fuelled spending spree to end anytime soon.

"French people are aware of the country's high public debt. But debt remains an abstract concept if its consequences are barely felt in everyday life. According to INSEE (the French national statistics agency — the ed.), 56% of the population receive more in government benefits and services than they pay in taxes and social contributions. The majority therefore have a tangible interest in maintaining the status quo," Charrier told DW.
For more than half a century, France has regularly spent more than it collects in tax revenue. The last time it balanced its national budget was in 1974.

France last paid a similarly high-risk premium at the end of 2011, during the eurozone debt crisis. What is particularly striking is how quickly it has risen: Since June 2026, the spread over German government bonds has more than doubled.

The main driver is not so much the general level of interest rates. Rather, it's the growing risk premium investors demand in response to high debt levels, political instability, large budget deficits and the recent unrest.

The higher the interest rates, the larger the share of the national budget that must be devoted to debt servicing alone. France is expected to pay more than €79 billion in interest on its total public debt in 2026. That figure is projected to exceed €91 billion in 2027 and could reach between €125 billion and €132 billion by 2030.

These figures include the costs incurred by social security funds and local authorities. The central government's interest bill alone is currently estimated at €62.6 billion by the Agence France Tresor, a French Treasury agency.

In the coming years, France will have to refinance large amounts of outstanding bonds that were issued when interest rates were at historic lows. At the same time, the country's substantial budget deficit means it must take on additional debt.
The trend of rising interest costs is also affecting Germany. The ZEW's Heinemann has calculated that German interest payments are likely to increase sharply by the early 2030s.

"For the federal government alone, which has so far paid around €30 billion, the figure will triple within a few years as both debt and interest rates rise. And it won't stop there — it will exceed €90 billion. Reaching €100 billion in annual interest payments in the federal budget is then no longer far off," warns the Mannheim-based economist.
